questions.q: How many main parts of speech are discussed in this topic?
o: Nine
Seven
Eight
Ten
questions.e: Nine main parts of speech are covered: nouns, verbs, adjectives, adverbs, prepositions, pronouns, conjunctions, determiners and interjections.

questions.q: Which four word classes are classified as lexical (open class) items?
o: Nouns, prepositions, pronouns, determiners
Nouns, verbs, adjectives, adverbs
Verbs, conjunctions, interjections, determiners
Adjectives, adverbs, prepositions, conjunctions
questions.e: The lexical items — those that carry semantic content on their own — are nouns, verbs, adjectives and adverbs.

questions.q: Why are lexical items also called "open class" items?
o: Because they only appear at the start of a sentence
Because they never change form
Because they accept new members as the language grows
Because they cannot stand alone in a sentence
questions.e: Lexical items are called open class because they readily accept new members — new nouns and verbs enter English regularly.

questions.q: Which five word classes are classified as non-lexical (closed class) items?
o: Nouns, verbs, adjectives, adverbs, determiners
Verbs, nouns, prepositions, pronouns, adverbs
Adjectives, adverbs, conjunctions, nouns, verbs
Prepositions, pronouns, conjunctions, determiners, interjections
questions.e: The non-lexical (closed class) items are prepositions, pronouns, conjunctions, determiners and interjections.

questions.q: What distinguishes non-lexical (closed class) items from lexical items?
o: They do not carry semantic content on their own and get meaning mainly from the lexical words in context
They carry semantic content on their own, just like nouns and verbs do in ordinary sentences
They always end in a recognisable suffix that marks them as belonging to a fixed word class
They can never occur at the start of a sentence under any circumstances whatsoever
questions.e: Non-lexical items do not carry meaning by themselves; they get their meaning mainly from the lexical words around them in context, and they do not accept new members.

questions.q: By what three criteria can each lexical item be defined, according to this topic?
o: Spelling, pronunciation and length
Form, position and function
Tense, number and gender
Origin, register and dialect
questions.e: Each lexical item is defined by its form (the shape it can take), its position (what it occurs with in sentences) and its function (its role in the sentence).

questions.q: How is a noun defined in this topic?
o: A word that expresses an action
A word that links two clauses
A word that names people, places or things
A word that modifies a verb
questions.e: A noun is a word that names people, places or things.

questions.q: Which suffix is illustrated by the words teacher, preacher, player and writer?
o: -ion
-hood
-ness
-er
questions.e: Words ending in -er, such as teacher, preacher, player and writer, are often identifiable as nouns.

questions.q: Which suffix is illustrated by the words nation, consultation and meditation?
o: -ion
-or
-hood
-er
questions.e: The suffix -ion, as in nation, consultation and meditation, is a common noun-forming suffix.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the noun-forming suffixes given in this topic?
o: -ness
-ous
-hood
-or
questions.e: -ous (as in famous) is an adjective-forming suffix, not one of the noun suffixes listed (-er, -ion, -or, -ness, -hood).

questions.q: How do most count nouns form their plural?
o: By adding -ies
By adding -es only
By adding -s
By staying unchanged
questions.e: Most count nouns form their plural simply by adding "s" — e.g. book–books, pen–pens, dog–dogs.

questions.q: How do nouns ending in "y" after a consonant form their plural, e.g. lady, country, baby?
o: By adding -s directly onto the unchanged singular form
By adding -es directly onto the unchanged singular form
By doubling the final consonant before adding a suffix
By dropping the "y" and adding "ies" to the remaining stem
questions.e: Nouns ending in "y" that follow a consonant drop the "y" and add "ies": lady–ladies, country–countries, baby–babies, pantry–pantries.

questions.q: Which group of nouns forms its plural by adding "es"?
o: Nouns ending in "o", "ss", "sh", "ch" or "x"
Nouns ending in a vowel followed by "y", such as toys and boys
Nouns ending in "er", such as teacher and player
Nouns ending in a silent "e", such as house and horse
questions.e: Nouns ending in "o", "ss", "sh", "ch" or "x" add "es": mango–mangoes, kiss–kisses, brush–brushes, church–churches, box–boxes (with some exceptions like photos and pianos).

questions.q: Which of these nouns keeps the same form whether singular or plural?
o: Book
News
Lady
Church
questions.e: Some non-count nouns, such as news, luggage and knowledge, retain the same form in both singular and plural.

questions.q: How does a singular noun ending in "s", such as James, most commonly show possession?
o: By adding only an apostrophe after the final s
By adding "of" before the noun instead of a suffix
By adding an apostrophe and an "s", or sometimes just an apostrophe
By changing the noun entirely into a new word
questions.e: Singular nouns ending in "s" (or not) typically show possession with 's, e.g. James's bag, though James' bag is also acceptable.

questions.q: How does a plural noun that already ends in "s", such as players, show possession?
o: By adding 's, e.g. "the players's ball", which is not the standard form
By adding "of" before the noun instead of a possessive suffix
No possessive form is possible for a plural noun ending in s
By adding an apostrophe alone, e.g. "the players' ball"
questions.e: Plural nouns that end in "s" show possession by adding only an apostrophe: the players' ball.

questions.q: How does a plural noun that does NOT end in "s", such as children, show possession?
o: By adding 's, e.g. "the children's ball"
By adding an apostrophe alone, with no added s
It cannot show possession in any construction
By adding "es" as if forming a plural
questions.e: Plural nouns that do not end in "s", like children, show possession by adding 's: the children's ball.

questions.q: Where do most common nouns occur in a phrase, according to this topic?
o: Before a determiner, at the start of the phrase
After a determiner, such as a, an, the, his, hers
At the very end of every sentence, after the verb
Only after a preposition, never elsewhere
questions.e: Most common nouns come after determiners such as a, an, the, his, hers.

questions.q: How are verbs broadly described in this topic?
o: Words that only describe nouns and never anything else
Words that only link clauses together in a sentence
Action words, though they can also express states and processes
Words that only precede nouns and modify them
questions.e: Verbs are described as action words, though they can also express states (He is a good man) and processes (Babies grow).

questions.q: What is meant by "tense" in relation to verb form?
o: The number of syllables in a verb
The emotional intensity of a sentence
The order of words in a sentence
The shape a verb takes to indicate distinctions in time
questions.e: Tense is the shape a verb takes to indicate distinctions in time.

questions.q: The bare verb form (no structural change) is used with which subjects?
o: First person singular/plural and third person plural, e.g. "I eat" / "They eat"
Third person singular only, e.g. "He eats" or "She runs" every day
Only proper nouns used as the subject of the sentence, e.g. "Kofi"
Only pronouns in the objective case, such as him, her or them
questions.e: The bare form shows no structural change and is used with first person singular/plural and third person plural subjects, e.g. "I eat", "They eat".

questions.q: How is the simple present tense typically formed for third person singular subjects?
o: By adding -ing to the bare verb form
By adding -s, -es or -ies, e.g. "Esi carries the bag"
By adding -ed to the bare verb form
By using the bare form unchanged as it stands
questions.e: The simple present tense is formed with -s, -es or -ies for third person singular subjects, e.g. "Esi / she carries the bag."

questions.q: Besides present events, what else can the simple present tense express?
o: Only future events that have not yet happened at the time of speaking, such as tomorrow's plans
Only completed past actions with a definite end already reached before the moment of speaking
Habitual events, universal truths, actions simultaneous with the present, and sometimes future or past time
Only hypothetical situations that never actually occur in reality, such as pure wishes or fantasies
questions.e: The simple present tense can express present events, habitual events, universal truths, simultaneous actions, and even future or past time in certain contexts.

questions.q: How do regular verbs form their simple past tense?
o: By adding -ing to the bare verb form
By an internal vowel change within the stem
By adding -s to the bare verb form
By adding -d or -ed to the bare verb form
questions.e: Regular verbs form the simple past tense by adding -d or -ed, depending on the verb type.

questions.q: How do irregular verbs like "come" and "sit" form their simple past tense?
o: Through other structural changes, e.g. come–came, sit–sat, run–ran
By adding -ed as usual, the way regular verbs form the past tense
By adding -s to the bare form, the way third person singular is formed
They have no past tense form at all, in either speech or writing
questions.e: Irregular verbs form their simple past tense through structural changes rather than a regular suffix, e.g. come–came, sit–sat, run–ran.

questions.q: What is "aspect" used to show, as in "She is going to school" vs. "She has gone to school"?
o: Whether the subject is singular or plural in number
Whether an action is progressive or completed
The gender of the subject performing the action
The mood of the sentence being expressed
questions.e: Aspect, formed with -ing, -d or -ed plus a helping verb, shows whether an action is progressive ("is going") or completed ("has gone").

questions.q: Where do verbs usually occur in a declarative sentence?
o: Before the subject, at the very start of the clause, every single time it is used
At the very end of the sentence only, after every other phrase has already appeared
After the subject, beginning the predicate, e.g. "The chairman tabled the motion before the house"
Only after a conjunction linking two clauses together in the same sentence
questions.e: Verbs usually come after the subject and begin the predicate, as in "The chairman tabled the motion before the house."

questions.q: What defines a lexical (main) verb?
o: It always requires an auxiliary verb to appear alongside it in every clause it forms
It only appears in the passive voice construction of a sentence, never in the active voice
It cannot take a subject in front of it at all, under any circumstances whatsoever
It denotes the main action and does not require an auxiliary — it can stand alone, e.g. "She smiled"
questions.e: A lexical verb denotes the main action and does not require the presence of an auxiliary — it can exist alone in the sentence, e.g. "She smiled."

questions.q: Which three verbs make up the primary auxiliaries?
o: Do, have and be
Can, may, shall
Will, must, ought to
Need, dare, used to
questions.e: The primary auxiliaries are all the forms of the verbs do, have and be, which can also be used separately as ordinary action verbs.

questions.q: Which of the following is a modal auxiliary?
o: Have, a primary auxiliary verb
Might, a modal auxiliary verb
Do, a primary auxiliary verb
Be, a primary auxiliary verb
questions.e: Might is one of the modal auxiliaries, alongside can/could, may, shall/should, need, will/would, dare, must, ought to and used to.

questions.q: How is an adjective defined in this topic?
o: A word that names a person, place or thing
A word that links two clauses together
A word that describes a noun
A word that expresses strong emotion
questions.e: An adjective is a word that describes a noun.

questions.q: Which suffix identifies the adjective "faithful"?
o: -ic
-al
-ous
-ful
questions.e: "-ful", as in faithful, is one of the adjective-forming suffixes listed.

questions.q: Which suffix identifies the adjective "attractive"?
o: -ive
-al
-ic
-ous
questions.e: "-ive", as in attractive, is an adjective-forming suffix.

questions.q: In "Esi is bigger than Ama," what degree of comparison is "bigger"?
o: Superlative, comparing three or more items
Comparative, comparing two items
Positive, with no comparison at all
Postposed, coming after the noun
questions.e: "Bigger" is the comparative degree, formed with -er, used when two items are being compared.

questions.q: In "Esi is the biggest of them all," what degree of comparison is "biggest"?
o: Comparative, comparing only two items
Positive, with no comparison at all
Superlative, comparing three or more items
Attributive only, sitting before the noun
questions.e: "Biggest" is the superlative degree, formed with -est, used when three or more items are being compared.

questions.q: In "A hardworking player was on their team," what position does "hardworking" occupy?
o: Predicative position, after a linking verb like "is"
Postposed position, immediately following the noun
Appositive position, renaming the noun it sits beside
Attributive position, between the determiner "a" and the noun "player"
questions.e: "Hardworking" is in attributive position — it occurs between the determiner "a" and the noun "player", modifying the noun phrase.

questions.q: How is an adverb defined in this topic?
o: A word that modifies verbs, adjectives or other adverbs, answering how, where, why or when
A word that describes a noun only, never a verb, adjective or other adverb
A word that links similar grammatical units together, like a conjunction does
A word that precedes and modifies nouns directly, like a determiner does
questions.e: An adverb modifies verbs, adjectives or other adverbs, and answers the questions how, where, why or when an action takes place.

questions.q: In "He is faster than you," what degree of comparison does "faster" show, and with which suffix?
o: Superlative, with -est
Comparative, with -er
Positive, with -ly
Postposed, with -ic
questions.e: "Faster" is comparative, formed with the -er suffix, just as some adjectives are.

questions.q: Which suffix is commonly used to identify adverbs, besides -er and -est?
o: -ness
-hood
-ly
-ion
questions.e: Many adverbs are identified by the suffix -ly.

questions.q: What property of adverbs allows them to begin, end, or appear mid-sentence, as in "Usually, we go on holidays" / "We go on holidays usually" / "We usually go on holidays"?
o: Concord
Aspect
Inflection
Mobility
questions.e: Adverbs have the property of mobility, letting them occur at the start, end, or immediately after the subject of a sentence.

questions.q: What can happen if an adverb is not properly placed in a sentence?
o: It can cause ambiguity about what the adverb modifies
The sentence becomes grammatically impossible to say aloud
The verb automatically changes tense to the past
The noun loses its plural form entirely
questions.e: When adverbs are not properly placed, they can cause ambiguity — the advice given is to place the adverb next to the headword it modifies.

questions.q: In "Present your case carefully," what function does the adverb "carefully" perform?
o: Time, telling us when
Manner, telling us how
Place, telling us where
Frequency, telling us how often
questions.e: "Carefully" indicates manner — how the action is performed.

questions.q: How is a preposition defined in this topic?
o: A word that names a person, place or thing, like a noun
A word that expresses strong emotion, like an interjection
A word that links nouns, pronouns and phrases to other words in a sentence
A word that shows number and possession of a noun, like a determiner
questions.e: A preposition is a word that links nouns, pronouns and phrases to other words in a sentence.

questions.q: In "The book is leaning on the table," what is "the table" called?
o: The subject of the whole sentence
An appositive renaming the subject
A determiner modifying a noun
The object of the preposition "on"
questions.e: "The table" is the object of the preposition "on" — the phrase that the preposition introduces.

questions.q: Where do prepositions normally occur in relation to their objects?
o: Before their objects
After their objects
They never combine with objects
In the middle of their objects
questions.e: Prepositions normally precede their objects.

questions.q: In "The man whom we gave the book to," what has happened to the preposition "to"?
o: It has been dropped entirely
It has been separated from its complement
It has become a conjunction
It has become a determiner
questions.e: Here the preposition "to" is separated from its complement, an alternative construction to "The man to whom we gave the book."

questions.q: In "I bought a bag for him," what type of complement follows the preposition "for"?
o: A noun phrase
A gerund
A pronoun
A conjunction
questions.e: "Him" is a pronoun serving as the complement (object) of the preposition "for" — prep + pronoun.

questions.q: Which preposition of time is used for specific clock times, as in "The bus will leave at 4:00am tomorrow"?
o: On
In
To
At
questions.e: "At" is used to designate specific times, e.g. at 4:00am.

questions.q: How is a pronoun described in this topic?
o: An anaphoric element used to replace a noun
A word that describes a noun
A word that precedes and modifies a noun
A word that expresses strong emotion or excitement
questions.e: A pronoun is an anaphoric element used to replace a noun, e.g. "The lady opened the refrigerator. She opened it."

questions.q: In "Kofi gave the book to me," what position does the pronoun "me" occupy?
o: Subject position
Object position
Determiner position
Appositive position
questions.e: "Me" occurs as an object, following the preposition "to" in this sentence — pronouns can occur as subjects or objects.

questions.q: Which pronouns change form to indicate person, number, gender and case?
o: Demonstrative pronouns
Interrogative pronouns
Personal pronouns
Relative pronouns
questions.e: Personal pronouns refer to specific people or things and change form to show person, number, gender and case.

questions.q: Which personal pronoun is the singular first person form, as in "I am happy"?
o: You, the singular or plural second person form
They, the plural third person form
We, the plural first person form
I, the singular first person form
questions.e: "I" is the singular first person pronoun in English; "We" is the plural first person pronoun.

questions.q: Which pronoun points to and identifies a noun, such as in "This tastes good" or "Those are my friends"?
o: Demonstrative pronoun, pointing to a specific item
Interrogative pronoun, used to ask a question
Personal pronoun, standing in for a person
Determiner, modifying a noun directly
questions.e: Demonstrative pronouns (this, that, these, those) point to and identify a noun or pronoun.

questions.q: Which set of words are the interrogative pronouns used to introduce questions?
o: This, that, these, those, the demonstrative set
The wh-words: what, which, who, whom, when, whose
I, you, he, she, it, we, they, the personal set
The, a, an, his, hers, the determiner set
questions.e: The interrogative pronouns are the wh-words — what, which, who, whom, when and whose — which introduce questions.

questions.q: How are determiners described in this topic, citing Afreh (2006)?
o: Words that express strong emotion
Words that join clauses together
"Those little words that precede and modify nouns"
Words that only occur after a verb
questions.e: Determiners are described (after Afreh, 2006) as "those little words that precede and modify nouns," e.g. the, a, that, a bit of.

questions.q: Where do determiners occur relative to the nouns they modify?
o: After the noun they modify, following the head word
In the middle of the noun phrase only, never elsewhere
They never occur next to a noun in any construction
They precede nouns and noun phrases, and are always followed by a noun
questions.e: Determiners precede nouns and noun phrases, and are always followed by a noun — this is why they are said to mark nouns.

questions.q: In "The cat is mine," what function does the determiner "The" perform?
o: It specifies the noun "cat"
It shows quantity
It shows possession
It joins two clauses
questions.e: "The" specifies the noun "cat" — one of the three functions of determiners listed (specify, show possession, show quantity).

questions.q: How is a conjunction defined in this topic?
o: A word that names a person, place or thing, like an ordinary common noun does
A word used to join similar grammatical units, like words and words, or clauses and clauses
A word that modifies an adjective, the way an ordinary adverb usually does
A word that always precedes a noun, the way an ordinary determiner usually does
questions.e: A conjunction is a word used to join similar grammatical units — words and words, clauses and clauses, or phrases and phrases.

questions.q: In "The boy and the girl," what grammatical units does the conjunction "and" join?
o: Two full clauses, each with a subject and verb
Two prepositions in sequence
A phrase and a noun/word, joined side by side
A noun and a verb in a single unit
questions.e: "And" here joins "the boy" (phrase) and "the girl" (noun) — an example of joining a phrase and a word.

questions.q: Which conjunctions are given as examples that show contrast between two grammatical units?
o: And, so, showing addition or result
Because, since, showing reason
On, at, in, showing location or time
But and yet, showing contrast
questions.e: "But" and "yet" are given as conjunctions that show contrast between two grammatical units, e.g. "The girl is good but the boy is naughty."

questions.q: How are interjections defined in this topic?
o: Words used to express strong emotions or excitement
Words used to join two clauses together, like a conjunction
Words that always precede a noun, like a determiner
Words that show possession, like an apostrophe s
questions.e: Interjections are words used to express strong emotions or excitement, and can be a single word or a group of words.

questions.q: How are interjections usually identified in written sentences?
o: With a question mark, since they seek a response
With an exclamation mark, since they express strong emotion
With a semicolon, since they link two ideas
They are never punctuated in any sentence
questions.e: Because interjections express strong emotion, they are typically identified in sentences with exclamation marks, e.g. ouch!, hey!, shhh!

questions.q: What property do interjections share with adverbs, in terms of position?
o: Both must always start the sentence they appear in
Both must always end the sentence they appear in
Both are very mobile — their position in a sentence can change
Neither can ever stand alone as a complete utterance
questions.e: Like adverbs, interjections are very mobile — their position in a sentence can change.

questions.q: The word "ambiguity" comes from which language, and what does its root word mean?
o: Greek, meaning "uncertain"
Latin, meaning "clear"
French, meaning "double"
Greek, meaning "hidden"
questions.e: Ambiguity comes from the Greek word ambiguus, meaning "uncertain" — uncertainty in meaning.

questions.q: According to the definition used in this course, when is a word, phrase, clause or sentence considered ambiguous?
o: When it uses vocabulary that is unusually difficult or technical
When it can reasonably be interpreted in more than one way
When it is grammatically incorrect according to standard rules
When it runs longer than a single line of text
questions.e: A word, phrase, clause or sentence is ambiguous if it can reasonably be interpreted in more than one way (Afreh, 2024).

questions.q: What is intentional ambiguity?
o: Ambiguity that only ever occurs in legal or contract documents
Ambiguity caused entirely by careless spelling mistakes
Ambiguity created deliberately, often for stylistic or persuasive effect
Ambiguity that can never be resolved by surrounding context
questions.e: Intentional ambiguity is ambiguity created deliberately, and is commonly found in advertisements and literature.

questions.q: In the advertisement "I like the sprite in you," what two meanings create the intentional ambiguity?
o: Sprite as a fairy, or sprite as a computer graphic
Spite versus sprite, a near-homophone confusion
Sprite as a verb, and sprite as an adjective form
Sprite the soft drink brand, or spirit as in one's inner character
questions.e: The line plays on "Sprite" (the drink brand) sounding like "spirit," so it can mean either the drink or one's inner spirit is being praised.

questions.q: In Keats's line "Thou still unravished bride of quietness," what two meanings of "still" create the ambiguity?
o: "Still" meaning "unmoving/motionless," or "still" meaning "not yet changed"
"Still" as a type of alcohol distillery, or as an adverb of time
"Still" meaning "silent," or "still" meaning "loud"
"Still" meaning "forever," or "still" meaning "never"
questions.e: "Still" in the Keats line can mean either "unmoving/motionless" or "not yet changed," both plausible readings in the poem.

questions.q: What is unintentional ambiguity?
o: Ambiguity deliberately created for advertising effect and persuasion
The unconscious use of ambiguous expressions, being unclear or inexact
Ambiguity that only ever appears in poetry and song lyrics
Ambiguity that is always grammatically incorrect in form
questions.e: Unintentional ambiguity is the unconscious use of ambiguous expressions — the writer or speaker is unclear or inexact without meaning to be.

questions.q: How many broad types of ambiguity does this topic identify?
o: Four broad types, in total
Three broad types, in total
Two — Lexical and Structural
Five broad types, in total
questions.e: The topic identifies two broad types of ambiguity: Lexical ambiguity and Structural ambiguity.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example most associated with intentional ambiguity rather than unintentional ambiguity?
o: A misplaced frequency adverb in an essay
An unclear pronoun reference in a report
A misrelated construction in a student's exam script
A pun used deliberately in an advertisement or poem
questions.e: Deliberate wordplay such as puns in advertisements or poetry is a hallmark of intentional ambiguity, used for stylistic effect.

questions.q: Most of this topic, after the discussion of intentional vs. unintentional ambiguity, focuses on eliminating which kind of ambiguity from writing?
o: Unintentional ambiguity that confuses readers
Intentional ambiguity used for advertising
Ambiguity found only in poetry
Ambiguity that cannot be corrected
questions.e: The bulk of the topic (lexical and structural ambiguity, misrelated constructions) addresses unintentional ambiguity, which good writers aim to eliminate.

questions.q: What is lexical ambiguity?
o: Ambiguity caused by punctuation errors
Ambiguity at the level of the lexical items of a language
Ambiguity that only occurs in questions
Ambiguity caused by sentence length
questions.e: Lexical ambiguity is ambiguity at the level of the lexical items of a language — i.e. individual words.

questions.q: Phonological ambiguity is caused by which kind of word pair?
o: Antonyms — words with opposite meanings
Synonyms — words with the same meaning
Homophones — same pronunciation, different meanings
Homonyms — same spelling, same pronunciation
questions.e: Phonological ambiguity is caused by homophones: words with the same pronunciation but different meanings (and usually different spellings).

questions.q: Semantic ambiguity is caused by which kind of word pair?
o: Homophones — same sound, different spelling, like the pair flower and flour in English
Compound words formed by joining two smaller words together into one single unit
Loan words borrowed wholesale from other languages into everyday English usage
Homonyms — same form/spelling and same pronunciation, but different meanings in different contexts
questions.e: Semantic ambiguity is caused by homonyms: words with the same form/spelling and pronunciation, but different meanings depending on context.

questions.q: Which of the following pairs is given as an example of homophones (phonological ambiguity)?
o: write / right
bank / bank
tie / tie
watch / watch
questions.e: Write/right is listed as a homophone pair — same pronunciation, different spelling and meaning.

questions.q: Which of the following pairs is given as an example of homophones (phonological ambiguity)?
o: letter / letter
flower / flour
bank / bank
watch / watch
questions.e: Flower/flour is a homophone pair — same sound, different spelling, different meaning.

questions.q: Which of the following pairs is given as an example of homophones (phonological ambiguity)?
o: tie / tie
letter / letter
nose / knows
bank / bank
questions.e: Nose/knows is a homophone pair used to illustrate phonological ambiguity.

questions.q: Which of the following pairs is given as an example of homophones (phonological ambiguity)?
o: bank / bank
watch / watch
tie / tie
hear / here
questions.e: Hear/here is a homophone pair — identical pronunciation, different spelling and meaning.

questions.q: Which of the following pairs is used as an example of homonyms (semantic ambiguity)?
o: bank / bank
write / right
hear / here
nose / knows
questions.e: Bank/bank is a homonym example: same spelling and pronunciation, but meaning either a financial institution or a riverbank depending on context.

questions.q: Which of the following pairs is used as an example of homonyms (semantic ambiguity)?
o: flower / flour
tie / tie
hear / here
write / right
questions.e: Tie/tie is a homonym example — it can mean a necktie or a drawn score, depending on context.

questions.q: Which of the following pairs is used as an example of homonyms (semantic ambiguity)?
o: hear / here, a homophone pair
flower / flour, a homophone pair
letter / letter, a homonym pair
I / eye, a homophone pair
questions.e: Letter/letter is a homonym example — it can mean a written message or an alphabet character, depending on context.

questions.q: What is the key structural difference between a homophone pair and a homonym pair?
o: Homonyms are always longer words than homophones are, on average, according to this view
Homophones only ever occur in formal written registers, never appearing in ordinary speech
There is no real difference at all; the two terms are simply interchangeable in every context
Homophones share pronunciation but differ in spelling; homonyms share both spelling and pronunciation
questions.e: Homophones sound alike but are spelled differently (e.g. flower/flour); homonyms share both spelling and pronunciation, distinguished only by context (e.g. bank/bank).

questions.q: What is structural ambiguity?
o: Ambiguity resulting from how words are put together into phrases, clauses or sentences
Ambiguity caused by a single word's multiple possible meanings taken alone
Ambiguity found only in poetry and other literary forms of writing
Ambiguity caused by incorrect punctuation marks only, nothing else
questions.e: Structural ambiguity results from putting words together as structures — phrases, clauses or sentences — and is also called ambiguity in syntax.

questions.q: How many sources of structural ambiguity are identified in this topic?
o: Four
Six
Five
Eight
questions.e: Six sources (A through F) of structural ambiguity are identified: word ordering, unclear modification, ambiguous reference, ambiguous word/phrase, negative statement + reason clause, and frequency adverb placement.

questions.q: In "The minister decided to appoint a panel of independent doctors to examine his deputy on August 31," what causes the ambiguity?
o: The word "panel" has two separate meanings in this sentence, which causes real confusion for readers
The pronoun "his" is being used as a homophone here, sounding like another completely different word
The phrase "on August 31" could refer to the time of deciding, appointing, or examining, due to careless word ordering
The sentence uses a frequency adverb incorrectly here, in an oddly misplaced position within the clause
questions.e: This illustrates Source A, wrong/careless ordering of words: the time phrase "on August 31" is left unclear as to which of the three actions it modifies.

questions.q: "The Vice-Chancellor has refused to enter dirty students' halls" is used to illustrate which source of structural ambiguity?
o: Ambiguous word or phrase in a sentence
Negative statement followed by a clause of reason
Ambiguous reference created by pronouns
Unclear modification of a headword
questions.e: This sentence illustrates unclear modification (Source B) — it's unclear whether "dirty" describes the halls or is loosely associated with the students.

questions.q: In "He ate the meal on the couch," what is the source of the ambiguity?
o: Unclear modification — "on the couch" could attach to "the meal" or to the act of eating
Ambiguous reference caused by a single pronoun standing in for two separate nouns at once
Wrong placement of a frequency adverb somewhere within the surrounding clause
A negative statement followed immediately by a following reason clause
questions.e: This is an unclear-modification example: "on the couch" could describe where the meal was, or where he sat while eating.

questions.q: "Visiting friends can be boring" illustrates ambiguity because "visiting" can be read as what?
o: Either a noun or an adjective describing the weather
Either a gerund or a participle modifying "friends"
A homophone of "vesting", pronounced the same way
A frequency adverb misplaced before the main verb
questions.e: "Visiting" is structurally ambiguous between a gerund (visiting friends = the act of visiting) and a participle (friends who are visiting) — an example of unclear modification.

questions.q: "Take the items from the boxes and wash them" is ambiguous because "them" could refer to what?
o: Either the verb "take" or the verb "wash"
A homophone pair sounding identical
Either "the items" or "the boxes"
The minister and his deputy from before
questions.e: This is an example of ambiguous reference (Source C): the pronoun "them" could grammatically point to either "the items" or "the boxes."

questions.q: "When I tried to glue the handle onto the cup, it broke" is ambiguous because "it" could refer to what?
o: Either the glue or the person
The minister or the deputy
The panel or the doctors
Either the handle or the cup
questions.e: "It" has two possible antecedents — the handle or the cup — making this an example of ambiguous reference.

questions.q: "Mansa told her that she is next on the programme" is ambiguous because "she" could refer to whom?
o: Either Mansa or the other woman referred to as "her"
The audience watching the programme
A homophone of "Mansa" in this sentence
The programme itself, as if it were a person
questions.e: With two female referents present (Mansa and "her"), the pronoun "she" is ambiguous as to which one is next on the programme.

questions.q: "The shooting of the policeman angered the people" is ambiguous because it is unclear whether the policeman:
o: was a homophone of another word
was shot, or did the shooting
is a fictional or real person
was mentioned earlier by name
questions.e: This is an example of an ambiguous word/phrase (Source D): the policeman could be the one who shot someone, or the one who was shot.

questions.q: "The killing of the lady infuriated the family" follows the same ambiguous pattern as which other example in the source material?
o: "Josephine doesn't eat breakfast normally."
"Visiting friends can be boring."
"The arrest of the lady infuriated the family."
"When angry, one's pulse rate quickens."
questions.e: "The arrest of the lady infuriated the family" follows the identical structural pattern — the lady could either have made the arrest or have been arrested.

questions.q: In "I didn't give Ode the money because she is a student," what are the two possible readings?
o: Ode is a student; Ode is not a student at all, under either possible reading
The money was stolen from Ode; the money was later returned again to Ode
I like Ode very much indeed; I dislike Ode very much indeed, either way
I gave Ode the money but not for that reason; I did not give Ode the money, for that reason
questions.e: The negative statement + reason clause creates two readings: either the money was given (just not because she's a student), or it was withheld precisely because she's a student.

questions.q: "I didn't give Ode the money because she is a student" is an example of which source of structural ambiguity?
o: A negative statement followed immediately by a clause of reason
Wrong placement of a frequency adverb in the clause
Unclear modification of the following noun
Ambiguous reference caused by a single pronoun
questions.e: This is Source E: a negative statement ("I didn't give") immediately followed by a clause of reason ("because she is a student").

questions.q: In "I do not like him because he is clever," what is one possible reading of the sentence?
o: He is not actually clever at all
I like him, but not because he is clever
I have never actually met him before
He likes me because I am clever too
questions.e: One of the two readings is that I do like him, just not for the stated reason (his cleverness) — the other reading is that I dislike him precisely because he is clever.

questions.q: Which adverbs are specifically named as frequency adverbs whose placement can cause ambiguity?
o: Quickly, slowly, carefully, loudly
Very, quite, rather, somewhat
Frequently, usually, always, normally
Here, there, everywhere, nowhere
questions.e: The source material names frequently, usually, always and normally as the frequency adverbs discussed.

questions.q: Why is "*Josephine doesn't eat breakfast normally" considered ambiguous?
o: "Normally" is a homophone of another similarly sounding word entirely, causing all the confusion here
It contains an unclear pronoun reference that could plausibly point to more than one different noun
It is a negative statement with absolutely no reason clause attached to it anywhere at all
"Normally" could describe how she eats breakfast or how often she skips it, because it is placed after the verb
questions.e: With "normally" placed after the verb, it's unclear whether it describes the manner of eating or the frequency of not eating — the frequency adverb is wrongly placed.

questions.q: How would "*Josephine doesn't eat breakfast normally" be corrected to remove the ambiguity?
o: "Josephine doesn't normally eat breakfast."
"Normally, Josephine doesn't, eat breakfast."
"Josephine eat breakfast doesn't normally."
"Breakfast Josephine doesn't eat normally."
questions.e: Moving "normally" to before the main verb — "Josephine doesn't normally eat breakfast" — gives the single clear meaning that she usually skips breakfast.

questions.q: What is a misrelated construction?
o: A sentence containing a simple spelling error somewhere in it, nothing more
A sentence where modifiers are attached to constructions they are not supposed to qualify
A sentence that uses far too many homonyms all at once, confusing the reader
A sentence that is missing its main verb altogether, leaving it incomplete
questions.e: A misrelated construction occurs when modifiers are attached to constructions they are not supposed to qualify.

questions.q: In "Having been written, Leslie posted the letter," what is grammatically wrong?
o: "Posted" is used in the wrong verb tense for this particular sentence
"Letter" is used as a homonym incorrectly here, carrying the wrong meaning entirely
"Having been written" grammatically relates to "Leslie," not to "the letter" as intended
There is a missing frequency adverb somewhere in the clause that should be added
questions.e: Because the opening phrase must relate to the first noun that follows, "Having been written" grammatically describes Leslie, though the letter was what was written.

questions.q: In "While walking, his feet hit a stone," what is grammatically wrong?
o: "Stone" is ambiguous between two separate meanings altogether, confusing the reader
The sentence lacks a subject entirely, with no noun present anywhere in it
"Hit" is used as a homophone of "heat" in this particular context, sounding alike
"While walking" grammatically relates to "his feet," not to the person doing the walking
questions.e: "While walking" grammatically attaches to "his feet" (the first noun/pronoun equivalent that follows), even though it was the person who was walking.

questions.q: What is "the grammatical principle" that governs opening phrases like these?
o: Opening phrases should, with certain exceptions, relate to the first noun, pronoun or noun-equivalent that follows them
Opening phrases must always contain a frequency adverb somewhere within them, without any exception whatsoever
Opening phrases must never be more than five words long in total, no matter how the rest is written
Opening phrases must always be homonyms of the main verb that follows them later in the sentence
questions.e: The grammatical principle states that opening phrases should relate to the first noun, pronoun or other noun-equivalent that follows them, with certain exceptions.

questions.q: In "When sufficiently cooked, the next step is to add pepper and salt," what question exposes the misrelated construction?
o: "Who added the pepper?"
"When what is sufficiently cooked?"
"Why was salt used instead of sugar?"
"How many steps are there?"
questions.e: The sentence never names the food that is cooked, so asking "When what is sufficiently cooked?" exposes the missing subject.

questions.q: "When sufficiently cooked, the next step is to add pepper and salt" and "While walking, his feet hit a stone" are both examples of misrelated constructions caused by which source?
o: Misplacement of the subject
Ambiguous reference with pronouns
Omission of the subject
Wrong placement of a frequency adverb
questions.e: Both sentences omit the true subject entirely (the food; the person walking), which is Source A of misrelated constructions: omission of subjects.

questions.q: "Having been written, Leslie posted the letter" is an example of misrelated construction caused by which source?
o: Omission of the subject entirely from the sentence, leaving no true subject at all
Ambiguous word or phrase somewhere in the sentence, with two possible meanings
A negative statement paired directly with a following clause of reason
Misplacement of the subject — the true subject is present but in the wrong position
questions.e: The true subject of "having been written" (the letter) is present in the sentence but misplaced after "Leslie" instead of directly after the opening phrase.

questions.q: In "Trying desperately to think of an excuse, Naa's poor heart pounded against her ribs," what does the opening phrase grammatically relate to?
o: "Naa's poor heart," not Naa herself
"Her ribs", the part that pounded
"An excuse", the thing being thought of
Nothing, because the sentence is a fragment
questions.e: Grammatically, "Trying desperately to think of an excuse" describes "Naa's poor heart," though it was clearly Naa herself who was trying to think of an excuse.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the two sources of misrelated constructions identified in the source material?
o: Omission of subjects
Wrong placement of frequency adverbs
Misplacement of subject
Both A and B above are valid sources
questions.e: Wrong placement of frequency adverbs is a source of structural ambiguity (Source F), not one of the two specific sources of misrelated constructions (omission of subject; misplacement of subject).

questions.q: When a misrelated construction is caused by misplacement of the subject, what is the correction strategy?
o: Delete the opening phrase entirely from the sentence rather than fixing it
Add a frequency adverb directly before the main verb of the clause
Move the subject into the correct position right after the opening phrase
Change the whole sentence into a question form instead
questions.e: For misplacement of the subject, the subject is moved to the right position, e.g. "Having been written, the letter was posted by Leslie."

questions.q: How is "Having been written, Leslie posted the letter" corrected using the "move the subject" strategy?
o: "Leslie, having been written, posted the letter."
"The letter, Leslie posted, having been written."
"Having posted the letter, Leslie wrote it."
"Having been written, the letter was posted by Leslie."
questions.e: Moving the true subject (the letter) into position gives: "Having been written, the letter was posted by Leslie."

questions.q: When a misrelated construction is caused by omission of the subject, what is the correction strategy?
o: Introduce the missing subject explicitly into the sentence
Move the existing subject to a new position instead
Delete the main verb from the sentence entirely
Turn the whole sentence into the passive voice only
questions.e: For omission of the subject, the missing subject is introduced, e.g. naming what is "sufficiently cooked" or who was "walking."

questions.q: How is "When sufficiently cooked, the next step is to add pepper and salt" corrected by introducing the missing subject?
o: "The next step, sufficiently cooked, is to add pepper and salt," which is still unclear.
"When the meat/fish/rice is sufficiently cooked, the next step is to add pepper and salt."
"Pepper and salt are sufficiently cooked next," according to this version of the sentence.
"Add pepper and salt when sufficiently cooked next step," in this alternative ordering.
questions.e: Naming the actual subject (the meat/fish/rice) removes the ambiguity: "When the meat/fish/rice is sufficiently cooked, the next step is to add pepper and salt."

questions.q: How is "While walking, his feet hit a stone" corrected by introducing the missing subject?
o: "His feet, while walking, hit a stone."
"A stone hit his feet while walking."
"While Kofi was walking, he hit his feet against a stone."
"While walking, a stone hit his feet."
questions.e: Naming the person (e.g. Kofi) and restructuring gives: "While Kofi was walking, he hit his feet against a stone" (or his feet hit a stone).

questions.q: What are "absolute constructions," as an exception to the misrelated-construction rule?
o: Phrases that must always relate to the first noun that follows them in the sentence
Phrases made entirely of homonyms carrying double meanings in every case
Phrases that only ever appear inside negative statements, never elsewhere
Phrases that carry their own subject and are grammatically complete on their own
questions.e: Absolute constructions have their own subject built in, so they don't need to attach to the sentence's main noun — e.g. "That said, we can leave now."

questions.q: "That said, we can leave now" and "All things considered, he's very honest" are examples of which exception category?
o: Absolute constructions, with their own built-in subject
Sentence adverbials, commenting on the sentence
Participial phrases functioning as prepositions
Ambiguous reference, pointing to more than one noun
questions.e: Both phrases have their own built-in subject ("that"; "all things"), making them absolute constructions — an accepted exception to the misrelated-construction rule.

questions.q: What is a "sentence adverbial," as used in this topic's exceptions?
o: A word that must always precede the main verb somewhere in the clause, without exception
A construction that comments on or links the main sentence, rather than describing a noun
A synonym for a frequency adverb such as usually, often or rarely
A pronoun with an ambiguous or unclear reference to more than one noun
questions.e: Sentence adverbials comment on the main sentence or link it with other sentences, e.g. "Speaking frankly, he's very honest" — they are exempt from the first-noun rule.

questions.q: "Considering his age, he's very fit" and "According to the doctor, he's very fit" belong to which exception category?
o: Absolute constructions, with their own built-in subject
Sentence adverbials, commenting on the whole sentence
Participial phrases that function as prepositions or conjunctions
None; these are genuine misrelated constructions after all
questions.e: These are participial phrases that have become fixed prepositions/conjunctions in English ("considering," "according to"), so they need not relate to the following noun.

questions.q: Which of the following words/phrases is listed among the fixed expressions that are acceptable even though they appear "misrelated"?
o: Having been written, a participial phrase
While walking along, a participial phrase
Trying desperately hard, a participial phrase
Owing to, a fixed expression
questions.e: "Owing to" is on the list of acceptable fixed expressions (along with provided that, regarding, concerning, broadly speaking, etc.) that do not need to relate to the following noun.

questions.q: Which of the following is also listed among the acceptable fixed expressions in this topic?
o: Strictly speaking, a fixed expression
Having been cooked, a participial phrase
When angry, a shortened clause
Shooting of the policeman, an ambiguous phrase
questions.e: "Strictly speaking" appears in the reference list of acceptable expressions, along with "broadly speaking," "putting it simply," and "taking everything into account."

questions.q: What is unacceptable about "He showed the painting to the customer with large patterns," and how should it be corrected?
o: The sentence has a missing frequency adverb somewhere, so it is corrected simply by adding the word "usually" directly before the verb.
"With large patterns" is misplaced and should describe the painting; corrected as "He showed the customer the painting with large patterns."
"Customer" is a homonym that needs replacing entirely with a much clearer, far less ambiguous word choice throughout the sentence.
Nothing at all is wrong here; the sentence is already perfectly acceptable exactly as it is currently written and punctuated.
questions.e: As written, "with large patterns" appears to modify "the customer" instead of "the painting" — the correction moves the phrase next to "painting."

questions.q: What is grammatically wrong with "Feeling hot and thirsty, the fresh coconut milk tasted very good indeed"?
o: "Coconut milk" is a homophone of another similarly sounding word entirely, causing real confusion for readers
The sentence lacks a main verb entirely, making it read as an incomplete grammatical fragment
The opening phrase grammatically attaches to "the fresh coconut milk," which cannot literally "feel hot and thirsty"
"Tasted" is used here as though it were a frequency adverb, which grammatically it clearly is not
questions.e: This is a misrelated construction: the coconut milk, not a person, ends up as the grammatical subject of "feeling hot and thirsty."

questions.q: What is grammatically wrong with "Encouraged by high grades, working even harder seemed to make a lot of sense"?
o: "Grades" and "harder" are homonyms sharing the exact same spelling and pronunciation throughout
The sentence contains an ambiguous frequency adverb placed oddly within the opening clause
The sentence is a correctly formed absolute construction after all, complete with its own subject
"Working" cannot literally be "encouraged by high grades"; the human subject who was encouraged is missing
questions.e: The opening phrase needs a person as its subject (someone encouraged by high grades), but "working" — an activity, not a person — occupies that grammatical slot instead.

questions.q: What is unacceptable about "Writing desk for sale by a lady with Queen Anne legs," and where does the ambiguity lie?
o: "With Queen Anne legs" should describe the desk, not the lady selling it, as it is currently written
"Writing" is a misplaced frequency adverb sitting in an oddly wrong position within the phrase
"Lady" and "desk" are homophones sounding exactly alike when spoken aloud together
The sentence has no verb anywhere in it at all, making it grammatically incomplete
questions.e: As written, the phrase "with Queen Anne legs" appears to modify "a lady" rather than "desk," producing an unintentionally comic misattached modifier.

questions.q: How is punctuation best defined?
o: Non-alphabetical symbols used in writing for clarity and comprehension
Uppercase letters placed at the start of every sentence
Any symbol used purely to decorate a sentence visually
The set of rules for spelling long or difficult words correctly
questions.e: Punctuation is defined as non-alphabetical symbols used in writing for the purposes of clarity and comprehension.

questions.q: Is capitalization classed as a mark of punctuation?
o: Yes, it is one of the thirteen main punctuation marks listed and discussed in this course topic
No — not all symbols used for clarity in writing are punctuation marks, and capitalization is not part of punctuation
Yes, but only when it is used together with proper nouns somewhere in a sentence
No, because capitalization is used only in titles and headings, never elsewhere in a sentence
questions.e: The source material explicitly states that not all symbols are punctuation marks, and capitalization is therefore not a part of punctuation.

questions.q: Which of the following is one of the thirteen marks of punctuation listed?
o: Capital letter, used to start a sentence
Underscore key, used to divide words
Bracket, one of the thirteen marks
Asterisk, used to flag a footnote
questions.e: Brackets [ ] are listed among the thirteen marks of punctuation, alongside the period, comma, colon, semicolon, dash, hyphen, apostrophe, quotation marks, parentheses, question mark, exclamation mark, and underlining.

questions.q: Which pair of marks are BOTH classified as end marks?
o: Comma and semicolon
Colon and dash
Hyphen and apostrophe
Period and question mark
questions.e: The three end marks are the period (full stop), the question mark, and the exclamation mark — comma, semicolon, colon, dash, hyphen and apostrophe are not end marks.

questions.q: What is the defining feature of an end mark?
o: It comes at the end of a sentence and tells the reader when to stop
It only ever appears in direct questions, never elsewhere
It separates items in a list of three or more
It always indicates strong emotion or excitement
questions.e: An end mark comes at the end of a sentence and lets the reader know when to stop.

questions.q: In the sentence "Akosua B. Antwi," what role does the period after "B" play?
o: It ends the sentence
It follows an initial
It marks a decimal point
It shows doubt about the name
questions.e: A period is used after an initial, as in "Akosua B. Antwi."

questions.q: In the price "$2.50," what is the function of the period?
o: It marks an abbreviation
It ends the sentence
It acts as a decimal point
It separates two independent clauses
questions.e: The period is used as a decimal point, as in $2.50.

questions.q: Which of these correctly uses a period after an abbreviation?
o: Mrs,
Mrs;
Mrs:
Mrs.
questions.e: A period follows an abbreviation such as "Mrs."

questions.q: "Do you know the motto of KNUST?" is an example of which use of the question mark?
o: Ending a direct question
Showing doubt about a fact
Introducing a list
Separating two clauses
questions.e: A question mark follows a direct question, as in "Do you know the motto of KNUST?"

questions.q: In "The Gold Coast was renamed Ghana on a Thursday (?)," what is the parenthetical question mark showing?
o: That the sentence is a direct question
Doubt about whether the stated fact is accurate
Strong emotion about the fact
That the sentence needs a comma instead
questions.e: A question mark in parentheses after a statement shows doubt about the accuracy of that fact.

questions.q: "What a shock!" is an example of the exclamation mark used to do what?
o: Ask a direct question of the reader
Show doubt about a statement
Express strong feeling or excitement
Separate a list of adjectives
questions.e: The exclamation mark expresses strong feeling, as in "What a shock!"

questions.q: "I know someone who likes orange, pineapple, and banana" demonstrates the comma used for what purpose?
o: To set off an appositive
To set off an interjection
To mark a decimal
To separate items in a series
questions.e: Commas separate items in a series, as in "orange, pineapple, and banana."

questions.q: Which sentence correctly uses a comma in a date?
o: June 24 2010
questions.e: Commas are used in dates and addresses, as in "June 24, 2010."

questions.q: What is the purpose of the comma in the number "1,000,000"?
o: To separate items in a series
To keep the number clear and readable
To show doubt about the value
To set off an appositive
questions.e: Commas are used in large numbers to keep them clear, as in "1,000,000."

questions.q: "Yesterday, we visited the library." — what role does the comma play here?
o: It separates two independent clauses joined together
It sets off a direct quotation from the speaker
It sets off an adverbial at the beginning of the sentence
It separates a series of adjectives
questions.e: The comma sets off the introductory adverbial "Yesterday" from the rest of the sentence.

questions.q: "The Hen replied, 'My axe is sick.'" shows the comma used to do what?
o: Separate a series
Mark an appositive
Join two clauses
Set off a direct quotation
questions.e: A comma sets off direct quotation before the quoted words begin.

questions.q: "Aquarium workers love animals, so they rescue hurt ones." illustrates which comma rule?
o: Comma sometimes used between two clauses
Comma after a salutation
Comma separating adjectives
Comma before an indirect quotation
questions.e: A comma is sometimes used between two (independent) clauses, as in this sentence joined by "so."

questions.q: "Dear Uncle Jim," demonstrates which use of the comma?
o: In dates and addresses
After salutations in letters
To set off an interjection
Between two clauses
questions.e: A comma follows the salutation in a personal letter, as in "Dear Uncle Jim,"

questions.q: "I like the feel of cold, salty water when I go wading." shows the comma used to do what?
o: Set off an appositive
Mark a decimal
Separate adjectives
Introduce a list
questions.e: Commas separate coordinate adjectives of equal rank, as in "cold, salty water."

questions.q: Why is "We, requested that the road be resurfaced." incorrect?
o: It uses a comma splice between two clauses
It uses a comma before an indirect quotation wrongly
It replaces an omitted word incorrectly with a comma
It places a comma between the subject and its predicate
questions.e: A comma must never separate a subject from its predicate; "We" should flow directly into "requested."

questions.q: What is wrong with "The candidate stated that, he was against taxation."?
o: It uses a comma before an indirect quotation, which is unnecessary
It has a comma splice joining two independent clauses
It separates a series of items incorrectly
It misuses an apostrophe to show possession
questions.e: A comma should not be placed before indirect (reported) quotation introduced by "that."

questions.q: "The foreman told me to be there early, I told him I couldn't." is an example of what error?
o: A missing appositive comma around a phrase
A comma splice — two independent clauses joined only by a comma
An unnecessary comma before an indirect quotation
A misplaced apostrophe showing possession
questions.e: This is a comma splice: two independent clauses are joined only by a comma, where a stronger mark (period or semicolon) is required.

questions.q: In "Frank said, he would come to see me," what error does the comma make?
o: It separates a series incorrectly
It marks a decimal incorrectly
It indiscriminately replaces the omitted word "that"
It sets off an unnecessary appositive
questions.e: The comma is incorrectly used to replace the omitted connective word "that" ("Frank said that he would come to see me").

questions.q: What is the general rule for when a comma should be used at all?
o: Whenever a sentence runs unusually long
Only in dates, addresses, and series of items
In any situation, as often as possible, for rhythm
Only in any situation where it adds to clarity and understanding
questions.e: A comma should not be used in any situation unless it adds to clarity and understanding — extra commas add clutter, not clarity.

questions.q: What is the primary function of the colon, as described in the source material?
o: To signal the reader to "watch for what's coming"
To separate items in a series only
To mark the end of a sentence
To join two words into a compound
questions.e: The colon is a mark of expectation or addition; its primary function is to signal the reader to "watch for what's coming."

questions.q: "This is my problem: what do I do now?" illustrates the colon used to do what?
o: Separate a preposition from its object noun in the phrase
Introduce a word, phrase, or clause after an introductory statement
Join two independent clauses of exactly equal rank together
Mark an appositive phrase sitting beside a noun
questions.e: The colon introduces a clause following the introductory statement "This is my problem."

questions.q: Which is the correct use of the colon before a long, formal quotation?
o: Placing a comma after the introductory words instead of a colon in this case
Never using any punctuation before a formal quotation at all, under any circumstance
Separating introductory words from the long or formal quotation which follows, using a colon
Using a semicolon before the quotation begins instead of the colon
questions.e: A colon separates introductory words from a long or formal quotation that follows, as in Jefferson's inaugural address example.

questions.q: "Dear Mr. James:" shows the colon used in which special situation?
o: Chapters and verses of the Bible
Volume and page references
Hour and minute figures
Business letter salutation
questions.e: A colon follows the salutation in a business letter, as in "Dear Mr. James:"

questions.q: "The English Novel: A Panorama" demonstrates the colon used for what purpose?
o: Titles and subtitles of books
Hour and minute figures
Bible chapter and verse references
Business letter salutations
questions.e: A colon separates a title from its subtitle, as in "The English Novel: A Panorama."

questions.q: "10:15 a.m." is an example of the colon used for what?
o: Volume and page references
Hour and minute figures
Bible chapter and verse
A business letter salutation
questions.e: The colon separates hour and minute figures, as in "10:15 a.m."

questions.q: "Exodus, 12:31" illustrates the colon used in which special situation?
o: Hour and minute figures
Business letter salutation
Chapters and verses of the Bible
Titles and subtitles
questions.e: A colon separates chapter and verse numbers in Bible references, as in "Exodus, 12:31."

questions.q: "War and Peace, II:122" illustrates the colon used for what?
o: A business letter salutation
Hour and minute figures
A title and subtitle
Volume and page references
questions.e: The colon separates volume and page numbers in a reference, as in "War and Peace, II:122."

questions.q: How does the semicolon compare in strength to the comma?
o: It is a stronger mark of punctuation than the comma, signifying a greater break or longer pause
It is weaker than a comma, signifying only a very brief pause somewhere here
It has exactly the same strength as a comma in every single possible use
It is stronger than a period, signifying an even longer full stop instead
questions.e: The semicolon is a stronger mark of punctuation than the comma, signifying a greater break or a longer pause between sentence elements.

questions.q: What is the key rule about what elements a semicolon can join?
o: It can join a phrase to a clause of practically any kind at all
It is used only between elements of equal rank — it is entirely a mark of coordination
It can join a dependent clause to an independent clause quite freely
It is only ever used inside quotation marks, never outside them
questions.e: The semicolon is used only between elements of equal rank; it is entirely a mark of coordination, not subordination.

questions.q: "If you make people think they're thinking, they'll love you; if you really make them think, they'll hate you." illustrates the semicolon used for what?
o: Joining a conjunctive adverb to a dependent clause directly
Introducing a formal quotation from another source
Separating independent clauses not joined by a simple conjunction
Marking a business letter salutation formally
questions.e: The semicolon separates two independent clauses that are not joined by a simple conjunction.

questions.q: "This job is not simple; however, it's exciting and rewarding." shows the semicolon used with which type of word?
o: A preposition
An interjection
An appositive
A conjunctive adverb
questions.e: The semicolon separates independent clauses joined by the conjunctive adverb "however."

questions.q: Which of the following is listed as a conjunctive adverb that can follow a semicolon?
o: Therefore, a conjunctive adverb
Because, a subordinating conjunction
And, a coordinating conjunction
Since, a subordinating conjunction
questions.e: "Therefore" is listed among the conjunctive adverbs (also, anyhow, besides, consequently, furthermore, however, moreover, otherwise, therefore, thus) used after a semicolon.

questions.q: When is a semicolon appropriate between two independent clauses even without a conjunctive adverb?
o: Only when the clauses are very short and simple
When the clauses are lengthy or contain internal punctuation
Only inside formal business letters
Never — a comma must always be used instead of it
questions.e: A semicolon may separate independent clauses that are lengthy or already contain internal punctuation, as in the Oscar Wilde example.

questions.q: What is the "no period, no semicolon" guideline used for?
o: Deciding whether to capitalize a word at the very start of every single clause you write
Determining exactly where to place a hyphen inside a long, awkward compound word
Checking whether a semicolon is justified — if a period couldn't correctly replace it, a semicolon shouldn't be used either
Deciding whether to use a colon instead of a semicolon in this one exact spot
questions.e: The safe guide is: if you couldn't put a period where the semicolon is, the semicolon does not belong there either.

questions.q: Why is "Inasmuch as Joe has a fiery temper; we have to be careful what we say to him." incorrect?
o: It should use a colon instead of the semicolon that appears somewhere here
It needs an apostrophe after "Joe" to show possession of the temper
It is missing an end mark at the very close of the whole sentence
The first part is not an independent clause, so a comma should be used instead of a semicolon
questions.e: "Inasmuch as Joe has a fiery temper" is a dependent clause, not an independent one, so a comma — not a semicolon — is correct here.

questions.q: What is the hyphen's basic function?
o: A mark of separation used between parts of a word
A mark used only at the end of quotations
A mark that always shows strong emotion
A mark used exclusively in business letters
questions.e: The hyphen is a mark of separation used between parts of a word.

questions.q: Which of these correctly uses a hyphen to join a compound word?
o: sisterinlaw
sister-in-law
sister in law
sister,in,law
questions.e: Hyphens join the parts of compound words, as in "sister-in-law."

questions.q: "fast-moving" and "half-asleep" are examples of the hyphen used for what?
o: Dividing a word at the end of a line
Marking a fraction such as one-half
Joining the parts of compound words together
Indicating an omission of letters
questions.e: These are compound words joined by a hyphen.

questions.q: According to the rules given, which word should NEVER be divided at the end of a line?
o: Structure
Alternative
Existentialism
Strength
questions.e: Monosyllables (one-syllable words) such as "strength" and "laughed" should never be divided.

questions.q: Why should "climbed" not be divided at the end of a line, even though it has multiple letters?
o: It contains a syllable with a silent vowel
It is a proper noun naming a specific person
It is a shortened contraction of two words
It is a word naming a unit of time
questions.e: Words should not be divided on a syllable with a silent vowel, and "climbed" is given as an example.

questions.q: Why can a word like "also" or "open" not be hyphen-divided at a line break?
o: Because it is a proper noun
Because it has only four letters
Because it names a unit of time
Because it is an abbreviation
questions.e: Words with only four letters, such as "also," "only," and "open," should not be divided.

questions.q: What does the dash primarily denote?
o: A list of related items
A possessive relationship between nouns
A sudden break or shift in thought
The formal end of a letter
questions.e: The dash is a mark of punctuation used to denote a sudden break or shift in thought.

questions.q: How should a dash be typed, since it does not appear as a single key on a standard keyboard?
o: As a single hyphen, with spaces placed on either side
As three hyphens in a row, with spaces around them
As an underscore character held down on the key
As two hyphens, with no space before or after them
questions.e: The dash is typed using two hyphens, with no space preceding or following them.

questions.q: "Do we—can we—dare we ask for more money?" illustrates the dash used to do what?
o: Indicate a break or shift in thought
Introduce a word for emphasis
Indicate omission of letters
Set off a business salutation
questions.e: The dash here indicates a break or shift in thought within the sentence.

questions.q: "What he needed most he never got—love." shows the dash used for what purpose?
o: To indicate a sudden shift in the writer's train of thought
To introduce a word or group of words the writer wishes to emphasize
To set off an appositive phrase describing a nearby noun
To show a comma splice error joining two clauses
questions.e: The dash introduces "love," a word the writer wants to emphasize by isolating it at the end of the sentence.

questions.q: "I think—no, I am positive—that you should go." demonstrates the dash used to do what?
o: Introduce a numbered list of items
Mark an abbreviation of a longer word
Set off strongly distinguished parenthetical material
Indicate a numerical fraction such as one-third
questions.e: The dashes set off the parenthetical, strongly distinguished aside "no, I am positive."

questions.q: "can't" demonstrates the apostrophe used for what purpose?
o: To form a plural of a noun
To form a possessive of a noun
To indicate an omitted number or letter
To form a shortened contraction
questions.e: The apostrophe forms the contraction "can't" (cannot).

questions.q: "A's" (as in getting several A's on a report card) demonstrates which use of the apostrophe?
o: Forming plurals of letters
Forming a singular possessive
Forming a contraction
Indicating omitted numbers
questions.e: The apostrophe is used to form plurals of letters, as in "A's."

questions.q: "class of '91" demonstrates the apostrophe used for what?
o: To form a shared possessive between two owners
In place of omitted numbers or letters
To form a plural of the noun
To form a singular possessive of the noun
questions.e: The apostrophe stands in for the omitted digits "19" in "class of '91."

questions.q: "sister's" demonstrates which use of the apostrophe?
o: Plural possessive
Shared possessive
Singular possessive
Contraction
questions.e: Adding 's to a singular noun forms a singular possessive, as in "sister's."

questions.q: "girls'" (apostrophe after the s) demonstrates which use of the apostrophe?
o: Singular possessive
Contraction
Omitted number
Plural possessive
questions.e: Placing the apostrophe after the plural -s forms a plural possessive, as in "girls'."

questions.q: In "Jim, Jeb, and Jerry's fish," referring to one fish the three of them own together, why does only "Jerry" take the apostrophe?
o: Because it is a shared possessive — ownership is joint, so only the last-named person takes the apostrophe
Because it forms a plural, not a possessive, of all three names taken together
Because Jerry's name is a proper noun rather than an ordinary common one entirely
Because it is a shortened contraction meaning "Jerry is" here in this sentence
questions.e: For a shared (joint) possessive, only the last name in the list takes the apostrophe -s, showing the item is owned collectively.

questions.q: Underlining is used for the titles of which kinds of works?
o: Songs and poems only, never any longer stand-alone works
Plays, books, newspapers, magazines, television programs, and movies
Single chapters of books only, never whole complete books
Short stories only, never novels, plays or films
questions.e: Underlining marks the titles of complete, stand-alone works: plays, books, newspapers, magazines, TV programs, movies, and CDs.

questions.q: "The Prince of Egypt" being underlined in a written reference indicates it is what type of work?
o: A short story, set off with quotation marks
A song, set off with quotation marks
A movie, marked with underlining
A magazine article, set off with quotation marks
questions.e: The Prince of Egypt is given as an example of a movie title, which should be underlined.

questions.q: What is the correct placement of a comma or period relative to a closing quotation mark?
o: Outside the quotation mark
It does not matter
Only exclamation marks go inside
Inside the quotation mark
questions.e: The rule for placement of punctuation is to put other marks such as commas and periods inside the quotation mark.

questions.q: "America the Beautiful" in quotation marks is an example of quotation marks used to punctuate what kind of title?
o: A song, set off with quotation marks
A novel, marked with underlining instead
A television program, marked with underlining instead
A newspaper, marked with underlining instead
questions.e: "America the Beautiful" is used as an example of a song title, correctly set off with quotation marks rather than underlined.

questions.q: What does the ellipsis (three spaced periods) indicate?
o: The formal ending of a written business letter
An omission from a quoted passage, or that a list continues
A sudden shift in the writer's train of thought
A shared possessive between two or more owners
questions.e: The ellipsis uses three spaced periods to show an omission, as in the Nkrumah quotation, or to mean "and so on" in an unfinished list.

questions.q: "There are 16 regions in Ghana: Oti, Ashanti, Bono, Central, Northern…" uses the ellipsis to mean what?
o: That the sentence is a direct question
That letters have been omitted from a word
"And so on" — the list continues beyond what is written
That the number 16 is being corrected
questions.e: Here the ellipsis means "and so on," signalling that the list of regions continues beyond what is shown.

questions.q: Which category of word should always be capitalized, according to the capitalization rules given?
o: Every noun in a sentence
Only nouns that begin a paragraph
Only nouns longer than five letters
Proper nouns and proper adjectives
questions.e: Proper nouns and proper adjectives — names of specific people, places and things — should always be capitalized.

questions.q: In "Ask Mother what we're having for lunch," why is "Mother" capitalized?
o: Because it is being used as the person's name, not just to describe the relationship
Because it starts the sentence and every sentence starts with a capital letter regardless
Because it is a title being paired directly with a proper name
Because it names one specific historical event from the past
questions.e: When a word like "Mother" stands in for the actual name, it is capitalized; when it merely describes ("my mother"), it is not.

questions.q: "Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr." illustrates capitalization of what category?
o: A historical event
A title used with a name
An abbreviation used alone
An organization
questions.e: Titles used with names, such as "Dr." before "Martin Luther King, Jr.," are capitalized.

questions.q: "Boston Tea Party" is capitalized because it falls into which category?
o: A geographic name
An organization
A historical event
A religion
questions.e: "Boston Tea Party" is capitalized as the name of a specific historical event.

questions.q: "Girl Scouts of America" is capitalized because it is an example of what?
o: An abbreviation
A historical event
A title of a creative work
An organization
questions.e: "Girl Scouts of America" is capitalized as the name of an organization.

questions.q: Which of the following pairs are capitalized as names of religions, nationalities, or languages?
o: Christianity, Chinese, Spanish
earth, sunday, march
doctor, teacher, engineer
north, south, east
questions.e: Christianity, Chinese and Spanish are given as examples of religions, nationalities and languages, which are always capitalized.

questions.q: Why is "Smile toothpaste" partly capitalized ("Smile" but not "toothpaste")?
o: "Smile" is simply the very first word of the whole sentence
"Smile" is the official/brand name, a proper noun, while "toothpaste" is a common noun describing the product
"Smile" is a title being used together with a specific person's name
"Smile" is an abbreviation standing in for a much longer word
questions.e: "Smile" is the official (brand) name and is capitalized as a proper noun, while "toothpaste" is a common noun and stays lowercase.

questions.q: Which sentence uses capitalization correctly, given the options: A) Have you seen "star wars"? B) One of the main characters is Princess leia. C) My favorite character is Yoda. D) I would like to have a ship like the millennium falcon.
o: Sentence A
Sentence B
Sentence C
Sentence D
questions.e: Sentence C is correct: "Yoda" is a proper name, correctly capitalized, and nothing else in the sentence needs capitalizing.

questions.q: What does the term 'concord' mean in English grammar?
o: Agreement between two units in a sentence in terms of number, person and gender
A type of punctuation mark used to end a declarative sentence, such as a full stop
The overall length of a sentence measured in the number of words it contains
A synonym for vocabulary or the choice of words a speaker uses
questions.e: Concord simply means agreement — an agreement between two units in a sentence in terms of number, person and gender.

questions.q: In the sentence 'The headmaster, who knew what must be done, asked the PTA to rally behind him', what type of concord links 'headmaster' and 'him'?
o: Verb-object concord
Noun-pronoun concord
Determiner-noun concord
Subject-verb concord
questions.e: There is agreement between the noun 'headmaster' and the pronoun 'him' in terms of gender — a noun-pronoun (gender) concord example.

questions.q: 'One of the alumnae told the students that she would support them.' What kind of concord does 'she' illustrate here?
o: Subject-complement concord, a rarer category
Adjunct-verb concord, based on time reference
Noun-pronoun concord in terms of gender
Verb-object concord, which is not a recognised type
