questions.e: 'She' agrees with the feminine noun 'alumnae' — this is noun-pronoun concord in terms of gender.

questions.q: 'Universities in Ghana must endeavour to help the communities that surround them.' Why is 'them' correct rather than 'it'?
o: Because 'communities' requires a singular pronoun to match
Because 'them' agrees with 'Ghana', the proper noun nearby
There is no rule involved here, it is simply a stylistic choice
Because 'universities' is plural, so the pronoun must be plural to match in number
questions.e: 'Them' agrees in number with the plural noun 'universities' — this is noun-pronoun concord in terms of number.

questions.q: 'The MP for one of the newly created constituencies promised that she would never disappoint her constituents.' What concord type does the change from 'will' to 'would' illustrate?
o: Verb-verb concord
Subject-complement concord
Determiner-noun concord
Object-complement concord
questions.e: Since the reporting verb 'promised' is past tense, the reported verb must also shift to past ('would') — this is tense harmony/sequence of tenses, a verb-verb concord.

questions.q: 'A lot of the phenomena discussed in textbooks in Ghana are alien to the students.' Which concord type is being illustrated by the choice of 'phenomena' over 'phenomenon'?
o: Object-complement concord
Determiner-noun concord
Subject-verb concord
Verb-object concord
questions.e: The plural determiner phrase 'a lot of the' requires the plural noun form 'phenomena' rather than the singular 'phenomenon' — determiner-noun concord.

questions.q: 'Two years ago, many students of one of the renowned universities obtained scholarships.' Why must the verb be 'obtained' rather than 'obtain'?
o: Because 'scholarships' is simply the object of the verb in this sentence
Because 'students' is plural, which controls the verb's overall form
Because the adjunct 'Two years ago' signals past time, requiring adjunct/adverbial-verb concord
Because 'universities' is treated as the true grammatical subject of the sentence
questions.e: The time adjunct 'Two years ago' establishes past time reference, so the verb must match with the past form 'obtained' — adjunct/adverbial-verb concord.

questions.q: 'They appointed him president of the association.' What concord type links 'him' and 'president'?
o: Verb-object concord
Determiner-noun concord
Subject-complement concord
Object-complement concord
questions.e: 'Him' is the object and 'president' is its complement; they must agree — this is object-complement concord.

questions.q: 'The Honourable Minister is the chairperson of the Ghana Peacelovers Union.' What concord links 'Minister' and 'chairperson'?
o: Subject-complement concord
Adjunct-verb concord
Verb-object concord
Determiner-noun concord
questions.e: 'Minister' (subject) and 'chairperson' (complement) must agree in number — subject-complement concord.

questions.q: 'The lecturer instructed the course representative to share a book to the students' contains an error of which concord type?
o: Tense-harmony concord
Verb-object concord
Subject-verb concord
Gender concord
questions.e: This sentence is used to illustrate verb-object concord — the relationship between the verb 'share' and how it correctly takes its object/complement.

questions.q: 'The chief of the town champions developmental programmes in his traditional area.' What concord type does the verb 'champions' illustrate?
o: Subject-complement concord
Object-complement concord
Subject-verb concord
Determiner-noun concord
questions.e: 'Chief' (singular subject) requires the singular verb 'champions' — subject-verb concord.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the three broad forms of concord discussed in this topic?
o: Notional concord, based on intended meaning
Grammatical concord, based on formal markers
Situational/pragmatic concord, based on context
Phonological concord, based on how words sound
questions.e: The three forms covered are notional, situational/pragmatic, and grammatical concord — 'phonological concord' is not a recognised category here.

questions.q: What is notional concord (notional agreement)?
o: Applying subject-verb agreement according to intended meaning rather than to syntax or form
Applying subject-verb agreement strictly by grammatical rule only, ignoring meaning entirely
A concord type used only with proper nouns like people's names or place names
A rule that ignores the subject entirely and looks only at the following main verb
questions.e: Notional concord applies subject-verb agreement rules according to the intended meaning of the noun rather than its grammatical form.

questions.q: Why is notional concord described as 'subjective'?
o: Because it never follows any pattern at all in practice
Because the number of the subject is determined by the intention of the speaker
Because it only applies to pronouns, never to full nouns
Because it is taught only as an opinion, not as a fixed rule
questions.e: Notional concord is subjective because the subject's number is decided by what the speaker intends to communicate, not by a fixed rule.

questions.q: Which type of noun is the classic example used for notional concord?
o: Compound nouns like 'toothbrush'
Proper nouns like 'Ghana'
Collective nouns like 'team' and 'committee'
Abstract nouns like 'freedom'
questions.e: Collective nouns such as 'team' and 'committee' are the classic examples of notional concord, since they can be singular or plural depending on intended meaning.

questions.q: In 'The committee are discussing a tight budget,' why is the plural verb 'are' used with the singular-looking noun 'committee'?
o: Because 'budget' happens to be plural in this particular example sentence
Because British English never ever uses singular verbs with the word 'committee' at all
Because 'committee' is always considered plural in English grammar, without exception
Because the speaker is thinking of the committee as individual members debating, not as a single unit
questions.e: The plural verb reflects notional concord: the committee is being conceived of as multiple individuals discussing, not as one indivisible body.

questions.q: What determines the number of a subject under situational/pragmatic agreement?
o: The context within which the subject occurs
The length of the sentence being spoken or written
Whether the sentence is phrased as a question
The speaker's mood at the time of speaking
questions.e: Under situational/pragmatic agreement, the number of the subject is determined by the context in which it occurs.

questions.q: What is a 'zero-plural noun'?
o: A noun that has no plural meaning at all, ever
A noun whose plural form is identical to its singular form
A noun used only in negative sentences, never positive ones
A noun that cannot ever be the subject of a sentence
questions.e: Zero-plural nouns don't change their form between singular and plural — examples include series, aircraft and species.

questions.q: According to the -ics rule, when is a word ending in -ics treated as singular?
o: Only when it starts a sentence, as the subject
Never — -ics words are always treated as plural
When it refers to a principle, a system, or a field of study
When it refers to individual practices or specific activities
questions.e: Words ending in -ics are singular when they name a principle, system, or field of study, taking a singular verb.

questions.q: According to the -ics rule, when does a word ending in -ics tend to take a plural verb?
o: Only in questions, never in ordinary statements at all
Only when preceded by the definite article word 'the'
When it names a broad field of study or academic discipline
When it refers to individual practices, applications, or activities
questions.e: When an -ics noun refers to individual practices, applications, or specific activities/instances, it generally takes a plural verb.

questions.q: 'Statistics is a required course for doctoral students.' Why is 'is' correct here?
o: Because 'statistics' refers to a field of study, so it is treated as singular
Because 'course' is itself singular, and that alone controls the verb here
Because 'doctoral' functions as an adjective in this sentence, not as a noun
Because the whole sentence is phrased here as a direct question
questions.e: 'Statistics' here refers to the academic discipline/field of study, so it takes the singular verb 'is'.

questions.q: 'The statistics on child abuse are alarming.' Why is 'are' correct here?
o: Because 'statistics' means the field of study here
Because 'statistics' here refers to specific data/figures, which is plural
Because 'child abuse' is itself grammatically plural
There is no rule here; both forms are equally acceptable
questions.e: Here 'statistics' refers to actual data/figures about child abuse, so it is treated as plural and takes 'are'.

questions.q: 'Statistics show that divorce is a common practice in our society.' What number is 'statistics' being used as here?
o: Singular, because it is the sentence subject
Singular, referring to the subject/discipline
Plural, referring to multiple pieces of data
Neither singular nor plural — it is used as an adjective
questions.e: In this sentence 'statistics' refers to multiple data points about divorce, so it is plural and takes 'show'.

questions.q: What is grammatical concord?
o: A form of concord used only in formal academic writing, never in ordinary speech at all
Agreement between a subject and verb based purely on the speaker's own intended meaning
Agreement between a subject and verb determined entirely by surrounding context alone, nothing else
Agreement between a subject and a verb in terms of number, based on objective markers of singularity and plurality
questions.e: Grammatical concord is the agreement between subject and verb in terms of number, and is objective because it relies on markers of singularity and plurality.

questions.q: Why is grammatical concord described as 'objective' compared to notional concord?
o: Because it relies on clear formal markers of singularity and plurality, not on speaker intention
Because it applies only to proper nouns, never at all to common ones
Because it is used only in formal KNUST examinations and standard written tests
Because it has absolutely no exceptions whatsoever in any of its rules
questions.e: Grammatical concord is objective because there are formal (rule-based) markers of singularity and plurality involved, unlike the subjective, meaning-based notional concord.

questions.q: According to the important notes on S-V concord, to which tense does subject-verb concord mainly apply?
o: Past tense only, never the present tense
Present tense, mainly, with one small exception
All tenses equally, with no exceptions at all
Future tense only, never the present tense
questions.e: S-V concord is mainly applicable to verbs in the present tense, except 'to be' (am/is/are), which also has past-tense concord markers like 'was'/'were'.

questions.q: Regarding personal pronouns, S-V concord concerns only which persons?
o: First person only
Second person only
Third person pronouns only
All persons equally
questions.e: S-V concord concerns only third-person pronouns — it, he, she (and their plural, they).

questions.q: 'In the room are the boys.' What does this sentence demonstrate about subject and verb order?
o: This sentence is grammatically incorrect as written
'Boys' functions as the object here, not the subject
The subject must always come before the verb in English
The verb can come before the subject in some sentence structures
questions.e: This sentence shows that although the subject usually precedes the verb, the verb can sometimes come first, with 'the boys' (plural subject) still governing the plural verb 'are'.

questions.q: In correcting subject-verb disagreement, which direction does the correction proceed?
o: Backwards — you determine the subject's number first, then fix the verb
Randomly, whichever version simply seems to sound better to the ear
Only the object of the sentence ever needs to be corrected
Forwards, from the verb to the subject, in each and every case
questions.e: The correction is done backwards: the subject's number is established first, and the verb is then adjusted to match it.

questions.q: According to the S-V concord notes, what is the only sentence element that affects the verb's number?
o: The object of the verb
The subject of the sentence
Any adjunct placed near the verb
The complement following the verb
questions.e: Only the SUBJECT affects the verb — nothing else in the sentence determines the verb's number.

questions.q: What does the rule 'SS : SV' state?
o: A plural subject requires a singular verb
Subjects and verbs never need to match
A singular subject requires a singular verb
A singular subject requires a plural verb
questions.e: SS:SV means a Singular Subject requires a Singular Verb, e.g. 'The Doctor acts professionally.'

questions.q: What does the rule 'PS : PV' state?
o: Plural subjects never take verbs
A plural subject requires a singular verb
A singular subject requires a plural verb
A plural subject requires a plural verb
questions.e: PS:PV means a Plural Subject requires a Plural Verb, e.g. 'Serious students admire disciplined teachers.'

questions.q: Which of the following can function as the subject of a sentence, according to the topic?
o: Noun phrases, pronouns, nominal adjectives, and nominal clauses
Only pronouns and ordinary adjectives, nothing else at all
Only proper nouns, never common nouns of any kind
Only noun phrases, never any other grammatical unit
questions.e: Four units can function as subject: noun phrases, pronouns, nominal adjectives (e.g. 'the rich'), and nominal clauses (e.g. 'What he said').

questions.q: The singular/plural (number) opposition is characteristic of which class of nouns?
o: Proper nouns only, like names of people
Countable nouns only, such as book and books
Uncountable nouns only, like water or rice
Both countable and uncountable nouns, treated equally
questions.e: The semantic opposition of 'one' vs. 'more than one' (number) is characteristic of countable nouns only.

questions.q: When the plural marker 's' (or 'es', or an irregular variant) is added to a noun used as a subject, what does the subject become?
o: An indefinite pronoun
A singular subject
A plural subject
A nominal clause
questions.e: Adding the plural marker 's' to a noun used as subject makes it a Plural Subject (PS).

questions.q: A subject WITHOUT the plural marker 's' is classified as what?
o: An ungrammatical subject
A nominal clause
A plural subject
A singular subject
questions.e: A subject lacking the plural marker 's' is a Singular Subject (SS).

questions.q: On the VERB side, what does the marker 's' (or 'es') indicate?
o: Singular verb
Past tense
Future tense
Plural verb
questions.e: Unlike on nouns, the 's' marker on a verb (e.g. 'prays', 'sings') indicates a SINGULAR verb.

questions.q: 'The country belongs to all.' What is the subject's classification here?
o: Plural subject
Singular subject
Nominal clause
Zero-plural subject
questions.e: 'The country' has no plural 's' marker, so it is a singular subject (SS), correctly paired with the singular verb 'belongs'.

questions.q: 'The students visits the library everyday' contains which type of subject-verb disagreement?
o: The subject is missing entirely
Both the singular and plural markers are absent
Both the singular and plural markers are present
There is no error in this sentence
questions.e: 'Students' carries the plural marker 's' (PS) while 'visits' carries the singular verb marker 's' (SV) — both markers are present, causing disagreement.

questions.q: What is the guiding principle for resolving subject-verb concord according to the topic?
o: 'Always add s to the verb, no matter what the subject actually is'
'Ignore the subject entirely whenever the sentence is unusually long'
'Whichever version simply sounds better to the ear at the time of writing'
'One at a time' — exactly one 's' marker should appear, either on the noun or on the verb, never both or neither
questions.e: The guiding principle is 'One at a time' — the 's' marker should appear only once, either marking the noun as plural or the verb as singular, never both or neither.

questions.q: According to the basic rule on 'and', what happens when AND joins elements that jointly refer to one unit?
o: The structure selects a singular verb
The verb is omitted entirely
The rule does not apply to 'and'
The structure always takes a plural verb
questions.e: When AND connects elements that jointly refer to a single unit, the structure is treated as singular and takes a singular verb.

questions.q: 'Rice and soup with elephant meat is delicious.' Why is 'is' (singular) correct here?
o: Because 'rice' is always grammatically singular all by itself
Because AND here joins elements referring to one meal, treated as a single unit
Because 'soup' is treated as an uncountable noun in this sentence
Because 'elephant meat' alone governs the whole verb's form
questions.e: Rice and soup here form one composite meal, so the AND-joined subject is treated as singular, taking 'is'.

questions.q: 'Heaven and Haven Company Limited deals in building materials.' Why does this take a singular verb?
o: Because 'Heaven' and 'Haven' are both proper nouns used here
This is actually a grammatical error found within the sentence
Because AND is used within the name/title of a single company, which is treated as one entity
Because 'building materials' is treated as grammatically singular here
questions.e: When AND appears inside the name of a single entity (a company or book title), the whole name is treated as singular.

questions.q: 'The banker and teacher is approachable.' What does this sentence imply, and why is 'is' correct?
o: 'Banker' and 'teacher' are simply near-synonyms used here
The sentence contains an uncorrectable grammatical error throughout it
Two entirely separate people, so the plural 'are' should be used here instead
One person who is both banker and teacher, joined by AND under a single determiner, so the verb is singular
questions.e: With only one determiner ('the') covering both nouns, they refer to a single person occupying both roles, so the singular verb 'is' is correct.

questions.q: 'The banker and the teacher are approachable' differs from 'The banker and teacher is approachable' in what key way?
o: The doubled determiner signals two separate people, so a plural verb is used
The first sentence given is simply always wrong to write
Only the word order between the two versions differs
No real difference at all — both mean exactly the same thing
questions.e: Repeating the determiner ('the banker' and 'the teacher') signals two distinct people, requiring the plural verb 'are', unlike the single-determiner, single-person reading with 'is'.

questions.q: 'Power and might belongs to God.' Why is the singular verb 'belongs' used here?
o: This is simply a grammatical error present here in the source material itself
Because 'power' and 'might' are near-synonyms expressing one idea, so AND connects synonyms and takes a singular verb
Because 'God' is singular and directly controls the verb form used here
Because 'power' is always singular in every single context it ever appears in
questions.e: 'Power' and 'might' are synonyms joined by AND expressing a single concept, so the structure takes a singular verb, 'belongs'.

questions.q: Which four connectors are classified as correlative (compound) conjunctions in this topic?
o: along with, as well as, plus, with, the pseudo-conjunctions
and, but, or, nor, the coordinating conjunctions
neither...nor, either...or, not only...but also, whether...or
although, because, since, unless, the subordinating conjunctions
questions.e: The correlative conjunctions covered are neither...nor, either...or, not only...but also, and whether...or.

questions.q: What does the Proximity Concord Rule state for correlative conjunctions?
o: The verb is always plural regardless of the noun phrases
The verb agrees with whichever noun phrase is a proper noun
The verb always agrees with the first noun phrase
The verb agrees with the noun phrase closer to the verb
questions.e: Proximity Concord Rule: when correlative conjunctions connect noun phrases of different number, the verb agrees with the NP closer to it.

questions.q: 'Not only the teacher but also his students ___ the motto of the school.' Which verb form is correct under proximity concord?
o: Understand
Understanding
Understood
Understands
questions.e: The NP closer to the verb is 'his students' (plural), so proximity concord requires the plural verb 'understand'.

questions.q: 'Either the students or the lecturer ___ French.' Which verb form is correct under proximity concord?
o: Speaking, the participle form
Speaks, the third person singular form
Have spoken, the present perfect form
Speak, the bare plural form
questions.e: The NP closer to the verb is 'the lecturer' (singular), so proximity concord requires the singular verb 'speaks'.

questions.q: What does the Remote Concord Rule state for pseudo-conjunctions like 'as well as'?
o: The pseudo-conjunction itself is treated as the subject here
The verb agrees with the NP closest to the connector
The verb agrees with the NP that is far from the pseudo-conjunction
The verb is always simply omitted altogether
questions.e: Remote Concord Rule: with pseudo-conjunctions, the verb agrees with the NP far from the connector — the opposite of proximity concord.

questions.q: 'The teachers as well as the School Prefect ___ every term.' Which verb is correct under remote concord?
o: Traveling, the participle form
Has travelled, the present perfect form
Travels, the third person singular form
Travel, the bare plural form
questions.e: The far NP is 'The teachers' (plural), so remote concord requires the plural verb 'travel', even though 'the School Prefect' (singular) sits right before the verb.

questions.q: 'The students as well as the lecturer ___ French.' Which verb is correct under remote concord?
o: Speak, the bare plural form
Speaking, the participle form
Has spoken, the present perfect form
Speaks, the third person singular form
questions.e: The far NP, 'The students' (plural, NP1), governs the verb under remote concord, so 'speak' is correct — even though 'the lecturer' is closer to the verb.

questions.q: Why is it important to distinguish correlative conjunctions from pseudo-conjunctions before choosing a verb?
o: Because they follow completely identical rules in every single case, so it makes no real practical difference at all
Because correlative conjunctions trigger proximity concord while pseudo-conjunctions trigger remote concord — opposite outcomes
Because only correlative conjunctions are ever able to join two entirely separate subjects together at once
Because pseudo-conjunctions never actually appear anywhere at all in KNUST examinations or written tests
questions.e: The two connector types point the verb in opposite directions — correlative conjunctions use proximity concord (near NP), pseudo-conjunctions use remote concord (far NP) — so misidentifying the connector produces the wrong verb.

questions.q: Relative clauses are always introduced by which kind of word?
o: An indefinite pronoun, such as someone or anything
A coordinating conjunction, such as and or but
A relative pronoun, such as who or which
A preposition, such as in or on
questions.e: Relative clauses are always introduced by a relative pronoun: who, which, that, whom, or whose.

questions.q: What is the 'antecedent' of a relative pronoun?
o: Another name used for the main clause itself
The object of the sentence, following the verb
The verb that follows right after the relative pronoun
The noun that the relative pronoun replaces/refers back to
questions.e: The antecedent is the noun that is replaced by (or that the relative pronoun refers back to).

questions.q: What does the SSS pattern in relative clause concord stand for?
o: Singular Antecedent + Singular Relative Pronoun + Singular Verb
Same Subject, Same Structure, repeated each time
Simple Subject Sentence, a basic clause shape
Subject, Sentence, Structure, in that fixed order
questions.e: SSS = Singular Antecedent + Singular Relative Pronoun + Singular Verb, all matching.

questions.q: 'One of the students who ___ IT is here.' Which verb correctly fills the relative clause gap?
o: Reads, the third person singular form
Read, the bare plural form
Reading, the participle form
Has read, the present perfect form
questions.e: The antecedent of 'who' is 'students' (plural), so the relative-clause verb must be plural: 'read' (PPP pattern).

questions.q: Which full sentence contains NO concord error, based on the SSS/PPP and main-clause rules?
o: One of the students who read IT are here
One of the students who reads IT are here
One of the students who read IT is here
One of the students who reads IT is here
questions.e: 'Students' (plural antecedent) requires 'read' (plural RP-verb, PPP); 'One' (singular subject) requires 'is' — so 'One of the students who read IT is here' is fully correct.

questions.q: What is the complex subject formula given in this topic?
o: Subject + Object + Complement, the basic clause pattern
NP1 + Conjunction + NP2, joining two noun phrases together
S + V + O, the simple three-part sentence pattern
D Determiner + Pm1 Pre-modifier + H Headword + Pm2 Post-modifier
questions.e: The complex subject formula is (D) Determiner + (Pm1) Pre-modifier + H Headword + (Pm2) Post-modifier.

questions.q: 'The newly elected first female Vice Chancellor of KNUST, who is a Professor in pharmaceutical sciences, relates well with all manner of people.' Why is 'relates' (singular) correct?
o: Because the headword of the long subject is the singular 'Vice Chancellor'
Because 'Professor' is itself a singular noun sitting here
Because 'KNUST' functions as a proper noun in the sentence
Because 'people' is simply the nearest noun sitting to the verb
questions.e: Despite the long chain of modifiers, the headword of the noun phrase is 'Vice Chancellor' (singular), so the verb 'relates' is correctly singular.

questions.q: What distinguishes a simple subject from a complex subject?
o: There is no real distinction between the two of them at all, ever
A simple subject always contains one word; a complex subject contains more than one word
A simple subject is always grammatically plural in its number
A complex subject never has a verb following it anywhere at all
questions.e: A simple subject always contains one word (e.g. 'Mathematics'); a complex subject contains more than one word (e.g. 'The students from Togo').

questions.q: 'A number of the students ___ their rights.' Which verb is correct?
o: Has known, the present perfect form
Knows, the third person singular form
Know, the bare plural form
Knowing, the participle form
questions.e: 'A number of' always requires a plural verb, so 'know' is correct.

questions.q: '...but the number of those who do not ___ very alarming.' Which verb is correct?
o: Were, the past plural form
Have been, the present perfect form
Are, the present plural form
Is, the present singular form
questions.e: 'The number of' always selects a singular verb, so 'is' is correct.

questions.q: Which group of words are all indefinite pronouns that take singular verbs?
o: someone, somebody, something
students, teachers, lecturers
banker, teacher, doctor
news, physics, mathematics
questions.e: Indefinite pronouns built from one/body/thing — someone, somebody, something (and similarly anyone/anybody/anything, no one/nobody/nothing, everyone/everybody/everything) — all take singular verbs.

questions.q: 'Every computer, printer, and fax machine ___ marked for sale.' Which verb is correct, and why?
o: Are, because there are three separate items listed here
Is, because 'every' before items joined by 'and' requires a singular verb
Were, because the sentence is written in the past tense
Have been, because it is treated as a compound subject
questions.e: When 'each', 'many a', 'every', or 'many an' precedes subjects joined by 'and', a singular verb is used — hence 'is'.

questions.q: 'The politics in Ghana and Nigeria ___ different.' Which verb is correct, and why?
o: Are, because 'politics' is always considered a plural noun by its very nature
Is, because 'politics' always requires a singular verb form to be used here
Are, because context here refers to distinct political systems/practices in two countries, not one field of study
Is, because 'Ghana and Nigeria' is treated here as one single grammatical unit
questions.e: Although -ics words are often assumed to always be singular, context determines number here — 'politics' refers to distinct practices in two countries, so 'are' (not 'is') is correct.

questions.q: Ignorance of irregular plural/singular forms of words such as 'phenomenon/phenomena' and 'alumnus/alumnae' is identified as what?
o: Not relevant to concord at all
A form of correct grammatical concord
An acceptable stylistic variation
A recognised cause of concord errors
questions.e: Ignorance of irregular noun forms like phenomenon/phenomena and alumnus/alumnae is explicitly listed as a cause of concord errors.

questions.q: According to the topic, what are the two key steps for correcting concord errors?
o: Find the subject and verb and ensure they agree; ignore intervening words between them
Change the sentence's overall tense; remove every pronoun found in it
Add 's' to every noun found; remove 's' from every verb found there
Rewrite the whole sentence completely; consult a good dictionary
questions.e: The correction method is: find the subject and the verb and ensure they agree, and ignore all intervening words between them since they do not affect agreement.

questions.q: What is a sentence?
o: A group of words which expresses a complete thought
Any group of capitalised words
A word that names a person, place or thing
A punctuation mark placed at the end of a clause
questions.e: A sentence is a group of words which expresses a complete thought.

questions.q: What are the two main components of a sentence?
o: Noun and adjective
Subject and predicate
Clause and phrase
Verb and adverb
questions.e: Every sentence has two main components: the subject and the predicate.

questions.q: In the sentence "Kofi is my friend," which part is the predicate?
o: Kofi, which is the subject here
my, a possessive determiner
is my friend, the whole predicate
friend, part of the predicate
questions.e: "Kofi" is the subject; "is my friend" is the predicate — what is said about the subject.

questions.q: Sentences are grouped into four main types according to structure. Which of the following is NOT one of them?
o: Simple sentence
Compound sentence
Complex sentence
Declarative sentence
questions.e: Declarative is a functional type, not a structural type. The four structural types are simple, compound, complex and compound-complex.

questions.q: What is a simple sentence?
o: A sentence consisting of a single independent clause, containing one main idea
A sentence with two or more independent clauses joined together
A sentence made up of a dependent clause only, with no main clause
Any short sentence that happens to be under five words long
questions.e: A simple sentence consists of a single independent clause and contains one main idea, with a subject and a finite verb.

questions.q: Which of these is an example of a simple sentence given in the lesson?
o: When he came, we had already eaten.
The students always go church.
John bought the book and paid for it.
Kofi played his drum this morning but Ama didn't dance because Charles was not there.
questions.e: "The students always go church" is a single independent clause — a simple sentence.

questions.q: Can a simple sentence have a compound subject and still remain a simple sentence?
o: No, any second subject automatically makes it compound instead
No, a simple sentence must have exactly one single word as its subject
Yes — e.g. "The houses and the cars were damaged" is still simple
Only if the verb is also compound alongside the subject
questions.e: A simple sentence may have a compound subject, as in "The houses and the cars were damaged" or "The teacher or his student pays for the book" — it is still one clause.

questions.q: Which coordinate conjunctions are named in the lesson as joining independent clauses in a compound sentence?
o: because, since, although
when, while, until
who, which, where
and, or/nor, but
questions.e: The lesson names and, or/nor, and but as coordinate conjunctions joining independent clauses in compound sentences.

questions.q: "He neither swept the compound nor washed the car" is an example of which structural type?
o: Compound sentence
Simple sentence
Complex sentence
Compound-complex sentence
questions.e: This sentence joins two independent clauses (swept the compound / washed the car) with neither...nor — a compound sentence.

questions.q: What is a complex sentence?
o: A sentence with two or more independent clauses only, joined by and
A sentence with one independent clause and one or more dependent clauses
A sentence with absolutely no subject present anywhere at all
A sentence made only of dependent clauses, with no independent clause present
questions.e: A complex sentence has one independent clause and one or more dependent clauses.

questions.q: "When he came, we had already eaten" is an example of which structural type?
o: Simple sentence
Compound sentence
Complex sentence
Compound-complex sentence
questions.e: This sentence has one independent clause ("we had already eaten") and one dependent clause ("When he came") — a complex sentence.

questions.q: "Since you are the father, give him some advice" is an example of which structural type?
o: Compound sentence
Simple sentence
Compound-complex sentence
Complex sentence
questions.e: "Since you are the father" is a dependent clause attached to the independent clause "give him some advice" — a complex sentence.

questions.q: What is a compound-complex sentence?
o: A sentence with two or more independent clauses and one or more dependent clauses
A sentence with only one single clause in total, no more
A sentence with two dependent clauses and no independent clause at all
Another name simply used elsewhere for a simple sentence
questions.e: A compound-complex sentence, as the name suggests, contains two or more independent clauses and one or more dependent clauses.

questions.q: "Kofi played his drum this morning but Ama didn't dance because Charles was not there" is an example of which structural type?
o: Simple sentence
Compound-complex sentence
Complex sentence
Compound sentence
questions.e: This sentence has two independent clauses (joined by "but") plus a dependent clause ("because Charles was not there") — compound-complex.

questions.q: In "Students have cleaned up the beaches, and they have planted flowers in the parks so that the shores will look inviting to visitors," what makes this sentence compound-complex?
o: It has no subject present at all anywhere in this whole sentence
It has only one single clause that is simply repeated twice over again
It has two independent clauses joined by "and," plus a dependent clause introduced by "so that"
It has four independent clauses and no dependent clause present at all here
questions.e: The two independent clauses joined by "and" make it compound, and the dependent clause "so that the shores will look inviting to visitors" makes it complex — together, compound-complex.

questions.q: How many dependent clauses does a compound sentence contain?
o: Exactly one dependent clause
Two or more dependent clauses
At least three dependent clauses
Zero dependent clauses
questions.e: A compound sentence contains two or more independent clauses but no dependent clauses.

questions.q: Which structural type contains exactly one independent clause plus at least one dependent clause?
o: Complex
Simple
Compound
Compound-complex
questions.e: A complex sentence has one independent clause and one or more dependent clauses — unlike compound-complex, which needs two or more independent clauses.

questions.q: What is a declarative sentence?
o: A sentence that gives a direct command to someone else entirely
A sentence that makes a statement or declaration, expressing an opinion, fact, or judgment
A sentence that only ever asks questions of the reader directly
A sentence that always ends in an exclamation mark instead of a period
questions.e: A declarative sentence makes a statement or a declaration — a proposition expressing an opinion, a fact, or a judgment.

questions.q: The lesson notes that a declarative statement may be true or false, positive or negative. Which example is given as a FALSE statement?
o: Mondays follows Sunday.
Kwame likes Alice.
Two and two is/are three.
Kwame dislikes Alice.
questions.e: "Two and two is/are three" is given as an example of a false declarative statement.

questions.q: What is the basic structural pattern of a declarative sentence?
o: VS, verb before subject
V, verb alone
OSV, object first
SV, subject before verb
questions.e: Declarative sentences have subjects followed by verbs: SV(O)(C)(A).

questions.q: "The girl is clever" illustrates which declarative pattern?
o: SVC
SVO
SVA
VSO
questions.e: "Clever" is a complement describing the subject — SVC.

questions.q: Can a declarative sentence have no visible subject?
o: No, a subject is always grammatically required and stated
Yes — e.g. "Good to see you" implies "It's good to see you"
No, declarative sentences must begin with a proper noun
Only in questions, never in declaratives
questions.e: Declarative sentences may have no subject on the surface, e.g. "Good to see you" (It's good to see you) or "Serves you right" (It serves you right).

questions.q: In "John bought the wallet and (he) paid for it," why is "he" placed in parentheses?
o: Because it is simply grammatically incorrect as it is written
Because it should be capitalised at the start of the second clause
Because the subject can be dropped/omitted in the second clause since it is understood
Because it functions as an object here in the clause, not a subject
questions.e: The repeated subject "he" is understood and can be omitted, showing that declarative sentences may drop an already-established subject.

questions.q: Which of the following correctly demonstrates fronting the negative adverb "scarcely"?
o: Scarcely I visit my hometown these days.
I scarcely do visit my hometown these days.
Visit scarcely I my hometown these days.
Scarcely do I visit my hometown these days.
questions.e: "Scarcely do I visit my hometown these days" correctly inverts with auxiliary "do"; "Scarcely I visit..." is marked ungrammatical in the lesson.

questions.q: "I can hardly imagine what to say" becomes which correctly inverted sentence when "hardly" is fronted?
o: Hardly can I imagine what to say.
Hardly I can imagine what to say.
Hardly imagine I can what to say.
I hardly can imagine what to say.
questions.e: Fronting "hardly" inverts the auxiliary "can" before the subject: "Hardly can I imagine what to say."

questions.q: Which of the following is listed as another function a declarative sentence can perform, besides making a statement?
o: Only ever stating plain facts, nothing more
Asking a question, e.g. "You have paid your fees?"
Only ever making false or misleading claims
Replacing punctuation marks entirely in a sentence
questions.e: Declarative sentences can be used to ask questions, as in "You have paid your fees?"

questions.q: "I would love a cup of tea" is given as an example of a declarative sentence performing which other function?
o: Giving a command
Expressing prohibition
Making a request
Making a suggestion
questions.e: "I would love a cup of tea" is listed as a declarative sentence used to make a request.

questions.q: "You will leave the room now!" is given as an example of a declarative sentence performing which other function?
o: Expressing emotion
Asking a question
Making a suggestion
Giving a command
questions.e: "You will leave the room now!" is listed as a declarative sentence used to give a command.

questions.q: "God save the king!" is given as an example of a declarative sentence performing which other function?
o: Expressing emotion
Making a request
Giving a command
Asking a question
questions.e: "God save the king!" is listed as a declarative sentence used to express emotion.

questions.q: "You could be cooking" is given as an example of a declarative sentence performing which other function?
o: Giving a warning
Making a suggestion
Expressing prohibition
Asking a question
questions.e: "You could be cooking" is listed as a declarative sentence used to make a suggestion.

questions.q: What is an interrogative sentence?
o: A sentence that gives a direct command to someone
A sentence that always begins with the word "Let"
A sentence that asks a question and may demand an answer
A sentence with no subject present at all
questions.e: The interrogative sentence asks a question — sentences that may demand answers.

questions.q: What is the basic structural pattern of an interrogative sentence?
o: SV, subject before verb
V, verb alone
OVS, object first
VS, verb before subject
questions.e: Interrogative sentences in English have the structure VS(O)(C)(A) — a verb before the subject.

questions.q: In "Will she come?", what kind of verb is placed before the subject?
o: An auxiliary verb
A main verb only
An adjective
A relative pronoun
questions.e: The verbs placed before the subject in interrogative sentences are always auxiliary verbs, such as "will" in "Will she come?"

questions.q: In speech, how does a yes/no question typically end?
o: Falling intonation
Rising intonation
No intonation change at all
A pause with no pitch change
questions.e: In speech, interrogatives end in rising intonation if it is a yes/no question.

questions.q: In speech, how does a wh-question typically end?
o: Rising intonation, going up at the end
The same as a plain statement
Falling intonation, going down at the end
It has no fixed intonation pattern at all
questions.e: In speech, interrogatives end in falling intonation if it is a wh-question.

questions.q: What kind of answer does a yes/no question demand?
o: A piece of information such as a name or date
A full explanation of the situation
No answer is expected at all here
Simply yes or no, nothing more
questions.e: Yes/no questions are questions that demand yes or no for an answer, e.g. "Are you tired?"

questions.q: How are yes/no questions formed from statements that already contain an auxiliary verb?
o: By placing the auxiliary verb before the subject
By adding a wh-word to the front
By removing the subject entirely
By changing the verb tense only
questions.e: Yes/no questions are formed from statements by placing the auxiliary before the subject: "You have eaten" (statement) → "Have you eaten?" (question).

questions.q: What wh-words can be used to form a wh-question, according to the lesson?
o: and, but, or, nor, the coordinators
who, what, which, whose, when, where, why, how
because, since, although, the subordinators
let, do, does, did, the auxiliaries
questions.e: Wh-questions are formed with any of the wh-words: who, what, which, whose, when, where, why, and how.

questions.q: In "Ama sells rice" (a statement with no auxiliary verb), what must be introduced before the sentence can be turned into a grammatical yes/no question?
o: A wh-word, such as who or what
A subordinating conjunction, such as because
The "dummy do" auxiliary, inserted before the subject
A comma splice, joining two clauses
questions.e: Where there is no auxiliary verb in the statement, the auxiliary "do" (the dummy do) is introduced to match the inflected form of the verb before inversion.

questions.q: According to the lesson's step-by-step example, what is the correctly formed yes/no question from "Ama sells rice"?
o: Ama do sell rice?
Sell Ama rice?
Is Ama sell rice?
Does Ama sell rice?
questions.e: The steps are: Ama sells rice (statement) → *Ama do sell rice (dummy do) → Ama does sell rice (do matches singular form) → Does Ama sell rice? (question).

questions.q: Turning "The student attended lectures last week" into a yes/no question using dummy do gives which result?
o: Did the student attend lectures last week?
Attended the student lectures last week?
Does the student attend lectures last week?
The student did attend lectures last week?
questions.e: Since "attended" is past tense with no auxiliary, dummy do is introduced as "did": Did the student attend lectures last week?

questions.q: Which sentence is given as an example of an interrogative sentence used to give a command, rather than to ask a genuine question?
o: Isn't Ellen a beauty?
What are you looking at on your phone?
Would you read through the script for me, please?
Won't you have a glass of beer?
questions.e: "What are you looking at on your phone?" is listed as an interrogative sentence used to give a command.

questions.q: Which sentence is given as an example of an interrogative sentence used to give an invitation?
o: Can't you think?
Isn't it Abu who is praising me?
Won't you have a glass of beer?
Would you read through the script for me, please?
questions.e: "Won't you have a glass of beer?" is listed as an interrogative sentence used to give an invitation.

questions.q: Which sentence is given as an example of an interrogative sentence used to make a request?
o: Isn't it Abu who is praising me?
Won't you have a glass of beer?
Can't you think?
Would you read through the script for me, please?
questions.e: "Would you read through the script for me, please?" is listed as an interrogative sentence used to make a request.

questions.q: Which sentence is given as an example of an interrogative sentence used to express emotion?
o: Isn't Ellen a beauty?
What are you looking at on your phone?
Can't you think?
Would you read through the script for me, please?
questions.e: "Isn't Ellen a beauty?" is listed as an interrogative sentence used to express emotion.

questions.q: What is an imperative sentence?
o: A sentence that asks a question
A sentence that gives a command
A sentence that expresses surprise
A sentence with two independent clauses
questions.e: Imperative sentences are sentences that give commands.

questions.q: According to the lesson, in which situations are imperative sentences typically used?
o: Only in written formal letters, never in speech
Only when directly asking for information from someone
When giving a direct command, directions, instructions, or orders
Only to express strong emotion or surprise
questions.e: Imperative sentences are used when giving a direct command, directions, instructions, or orders — e.g. Stand up. Sit down. Go straight.

questions.q: "Close the door" illustrates which imperative pattern?
o: VA
VC
VOA
VO
questions.e: "Close" is the verb and "the door" is the object — VO.

questions.q: "Be a man" illustrates which imperative pattern?
o: VC
VA
VO
VOA
questions.e: "A man" is a complement describing the implied subject — VC.

questions.q: How are first and third person imperatives typically introduced?
o: By a wh-word placed at the start
By the word "let" before the subject
By an auxiliary verb placed before the subject
By a question mark at the end
questions.e: First and third person imperatives are introduced by the word "let" before the subject, e.g. "Let us keep off the grass" (first person), "Let them pay their dues" (third person).

questions.q: "Let me rest for today" is an example of which type of imperative?
o: Second person imperative
Third person imperative
First person imperative
Not an imperative at all
questions.e: "Let me rest for today" uses "let" plus the first-person pronoun "me" — a first person imperative.

questions.q: "Have a nice week-end" is given as an example of an imperative sentence performing which other function?
o: Making a threat
Giving a warning
Expressing prohibition
Making a wish
questions.e: "Have a nice week-end" is listed as an imperative sentence used to make a wish.

questions.q: "Let's share a cup of tea" is given as an example of an imperative sentence performing which other function?
o: Giving an invitation
Making a prohibition
Giving a warning
Making a threat
questions.e: "Let's share a cup of tea" is listed as an imperative sentence used to give an invitation.

questions.q: "Laugh again or I punish you" is given as an example of an imperative sentence performing which other function?
o: Making a wish
Making a threat
Giving an invitation
Making a prohibition
questions.e: "Laugh again or I punish you" is listed as an imperative sentence used to make a threat.

questions.q: What is an exclamatory sentence?
o: A sentence that asks for information
A sentence that gives a direct command only
A sentence that expresses surprises, emotions, or feelings
A sentence with two independent clauses joined by "but"
questions.e: Exclamatory sentences express surprises, emotions, or feelings.

questions.q: What punctuation mark do exclamatory sentences end in?
o: A full stop
A question mark
A semicolon
An exclamation mark
questions.e: Exclamatory sentences end in an exclamation mark.

questions.q: Which of the following is given as an example of an exclamatory sentence?
o: What a fantastic goal!
What is your name?
Let them pay their dues.
Since you are the father, give him some advice.
questions.e: "What a fantastic goal!" is one of the exclamatory sentence examples given in the lesson.

questions.q: "Aren't these girls beautiful!" is structurally similar to which other functional type, even though it is classified as exclamatory?
o: Simple declarative
Interrogative
Imperative
Compound-complex
questions.e: "Aren't these girls beautiful!" has the inverted verb-before-subject order typical of interrogatives, but functions exclamatorily because it expresses admiration and ends in an exclamation mark rather than seeking an answer.

questions.q: What is a sentence fragment?
o: A group of words punctuated like a sentence but that does not express a complete thought
A sentence joined together improperly by a semicolon in the middle of it
A question posed to someone that has no clear answer given anywhere
A sentence with more than one independent clause joined correctly in it
questions.e: A sentence fragment is a phrase or dependent clause punctuated like a sentence (capital letter, full stop) but that fails to express a complete thought or idea.

questions.q: Every true sentence must have which two elements, plus express a complete thought?
o: An object and a complement
A subject and a verb
An adjective and an adverb
A conjunction and a preposition
questions.e: A sentence must have a subject and a verb and must express a complete thought; missing any of these makes it a fragment.

questions.q: Which of the following is a sentence fragment?
o: The director walked into the office.
She wore a dark striped dress.
When I was going home.
Kofi is my friend.
questions.e: "When I was going home." begins with the dependent word "when" and never completes the thought — it is a fragment.

questions.q: "Whenever I am waiting for an important phone call." is an example of what kind of error?
o: A correctly punctuated complex sentence
A comma splice, joining two clauses
A fused sentence, with no punctuation
A sentence fragment, lacking a complete thought
questions.e: The clause begins with the dependent word "whenever" and is never joined to an independent clause, so it is a fragment, not a complete sentence.

questions.q: "Although I had never played soccer before." is a fragment because it:
o: Begins with a dependent word and is not attached to an independent clause
Has two entirely separate subjects joined together in the one clause
Ends with a question mark instead of an ordinary full stop
Has no verb at all present anywhere in it whatsoever
questions.e: The subordinating word "although" makes this a dependent clause; on its own, without an independent clause attached, it is a fragment.

questions.q: How many common types of sentence fragment does this topic identify?
o: Six
Four
Three
Two
questions.e: Four common types are identified: dependent-word, −ing, added-details, and missing-subject fragments.

questions.q: Which type of fragment begins with a subordinating word such as after, until, when, or although?
o: Missing-subject fragment, lacking a subject
Added-details fragment, adding extra detail
Dependent-word fragment, beginning with such a subordinating word
−ing fragment, starting with a verb form
questions.e: A dependent-word fragment begins with a dependent (subordinating) word and is left detached from an independent clause.

questions.q: "After I cashed my paycheck. I treated myself to dinner." is best classified as which type of fragment?
o: Added-details fragment, adding extra detail
−ing fragment, starting with a verb form
Missing-subject fragment, lacking a subject
Dependent-word fragment, beginning with a subordinating word
questions.e: "After I cashed my paycheck." begins with the dependent word "after" and is cut off from the clause it belongs with — a dependent-word fragment.

questions.q: What typically causes an −ing fragment?
o: An −ing word appears at or near the start of the word group, which often lacks a subject and part of the verb
The sentence simply has far too many commas placed throughout it in every clause
The sentence ends abruptly without any closing punctuation mark present at all
The word group begins with a coordinating conjunction like and, but, or or
questions.e: An −ing fragment arises because a word group starting near an −ing word often lacks a proper subject and the rest of the verb needed to stand alone.

questions.q: "Boatemaa walked all over the neighbourhood yesterday. Trying to find her dog." — how should this be corrected?
o: Trying to find her dog. Boatemaa walked all over the neighbourhood yesterday.
Boatemaa walked all over the neighbourhood yesterday trying to find her dog.
Boatemaa walked. All over the neighbourhood yesterday trying to find her dog.
Boatemaa, walked all over the neighbourhood. Yesterday trying to find her dog.
questions.e: Joining the −ing phrase to the sentence it belongs with removes the fragment: "Boatemaa walked all over the neighbourhood yesterday trying to find her dog."

questions.q: Added-details fragments often begin with which kinds of words?
o: Personal pronouns such as I, you, he, she, and it
Subordinating conjunctions such as because, since, although, and unless
Words like also, especially, like, including, except, for example, such as
Coordinating conjunctions such as and, but, or, so, and yet
questions.e: Added-details fragments typically begin with words such as also, especially, like, including, except, for example, or such as, and lack their own subject and verb.

questions.q: "Before a race, I eat starchy foods. Such as bread and spaghetti." — what type of fragment is "Such as bread and spaghetti."?
o: Dependent-word fragment, beginning with when or although
−ing fragment, starting with a verb form
Missing-subject fragment, lacking a subject
Added-details fragment, adding extra descriptive detail
questions.e: "Such as bread and spaghetti." begins with "such as" and has no subject or verb — an added-details fragment.

questions.q: "Akosua loved getting wedding presents. But hated writing thank-you notes." is an example of which type of fragment?
o: Missing-subject fragment, lacking its own subject
Dependent-word fragment, beginning with when or although
Added-details fragment, adding extra detail
−ing fragment, starting with a verb form
questions.e: "But hated writing thank-you notes." has no subject of its own — it needs "Akosua" or "she" to be complete, making it a missing-subject fragment.

questions.q: To correct a fragment, the first thing you should check for is:
o: The number of commas used
A subject and a verb
The presence of a semicolon
Whether the sentence is too long
questions.e: The first correction step is checking whether the word group has both a subject and a verb.

questions.q: "The dog in the pet store window." is a fragment. Which is a valid revision?
o: The dog, in the pet store window.
The dog. In the pet store window.
The dog in the pet store window has eaten.
In the pet store window the dog.
questions.e: Adding a verb ("has eaten") supplies the missing element and completes the sentence.

questions.q: "Your sister having all the skills required of a good salesperson." — which is a correct revision?
o: Your sister. Having all the skills required of a good salesperson.
Having all the skills, your sister required of a good salesperson.
Your sister having, all the skills required of a good salesperson.
Your sister has all the skills required of a good salesperson.
questions.e: Replacing the bare −ing form "having" with the finite verb "has" completes the sentence: "Your sister has all the skills required of a good salesperson."

questions.q: "The group is vibrant. Especially the youngest member of the group." should be corrected by:
o: Joining the two word groups with a comma: "The group is vibrant, especially the youngest member of the group."
Adding a semicolon between them without changing anything else at all in the sentence
Turning "especially" into a brand new subject for the whole sentence
Deleting "especially" entirely from the second word group in the sentence
questions.e: An added-details fragment beginning with "especially" is corrected by joining it with a comma to the sentence it belongs with.

questions.q: "will soon be sleeping." on its own is an example of which kind of fragment, and how is it corrected?
o: A dependent-word fragment; corrected with a semicolon added in near the start
A phrase fragment; corrected by supplying the missing subject, e.g. "The baby will soon be sleeping."
An added-details fragment; corrected by removing the verb entirely from it
A subordinate-clause fragment; corrected by adding a comma after it in the middle
questions.e: A phrase left to stand alone (missing its subject) is a phrase fragment; you correct it by supplying the missing element, here the subject "The baby."

questions.q: "After the candidates arrive." is a subordinate-clause fragment. How should it be corrected?
o: By deleting the word "after" only, leaving the whole rest of it unchanged
By adding an exclamation mark at the very end of the fragment
By joining it to an independent clause, e.g. "After the candidates arrive, the inter-halls debate will begin."
By simply repeating the whole entire clause twice over again
questions.e: A subordinate clause left standing alone must be joined to an independent clause to form a complete sentence.

questions.q: A run-on sentence occurs when:
o: A sentence has far too many adjectives strung together in a row
A sentence is missing its subject entirely from start to finish
A dependent clause is left standing all alone with nothing attached
Two or more independent clauses are joined without appropriate punctuation or the correct conjunction
questions.e: A run-on occurs when two or more independent clauses run together without the punctuation or conjunction needed to signal the break between them.

questions.q: Which of the following is a run-on sentence?
o: The bus stopped suddenly I found myself in an old man's lap.
The dog is in the pet store window.
Trying to find her dog, Boatemaa walked all over the neighbourhood.
After I cashed my paycheck, I treated myself to dinner.
questions.e: "The bus stopped suddenly I found myself in an old man's lap." fuses two independent clauses with no punctuation between them — a run-on.

questions.q: "We heard the noise in the garage two birds had flown in through the open window." is an example of what error?
o: A missing-subject fragment
A run-on sentence
Correct parallelism
A subordinate-clause fragment
questions.e: Two independent clauses ("We heard the noise in the garage" and "two birds had flown in through the open window") are joined with no punctuation at all — a fused run-on.

questions.q: "Akosua cleans her kitchen every week she shines every pot and pan." is best classified as:
o: A comma splice
A dependent-word fragment
A fused sentence
An −ing fragment
questions.e: There is no punctuation at all between the two independent clauses, so this is a fused sentence, one of the two types of run-on.

questions.q: How many main types of run-on sentence are identified in this topic?
o: Three
Five
Four
Two
questions.e: Two types of run-on sentence are identified: fused sentences and comma splices.

questions.q: What distinguishes a fused sentence from a comma splice?
o: A fused sentence has no punctuation at all marking the break; a comma splice wrongly uses a comma where a period or semicolon is needed
A fused sentence is always considerably shorter in overall length than a comma splice sentence ever is
There is no real difference at all between the two of them, not even a small one
A fused sentence uses far too many commas scattered throughout it; a comma splice uses none at all anywhere
questions.e: Fused sentences have zero punctuation between the independent clauses, while comma splices incorrectly use a comma where a stronger punctuation mark (period or semicolon) is required.

questions.q: "I studied for the test all weekend I am well prepared for it." (with no comma at all) is an example of:
o: A comma splice, using a comma instead of a period
A fused sentence, with no punctuation at all
An added-details fragment, lacking a subject or verb
A correctly punctuated compound sentence with and
questions.e: With no punctuation at all separating the two independent clauses, this is a fused sentence.

questions.q: How many standard ways of correcting a run-on sentence are given in this topic?
o: Six
Three
Four
Two
questions.e: Four standard correction methods are given: period and capital letter, comma with a coordinating conjunction, semicolon, and subordinating conjunction.

questions.q: Which correction method turns "The bus stopped suddenly I found myself in an old man's lap." into "The bus stopped suddenly. I found myself in an old man's lap."?
o: Semicolon alone, with no capital letter
Subordinating conjunction, added at the start
Comma and coordinating conjunction
Period and a capital letter
questions.e: Splitting the run-on into two separate sentences, each starting with a capital letter, is the period-and-capital-letter method.

questions.q: "The bus stopped suddenly, and I found myself in an old man's lap." uses which correction method?
o: A comma and a coordinating conjunction
A semicolon alone, with no capital letter
A subordinating conjunction, added at the start
A period and a capital letter
questions.e: Adding a comma followed by the coordinating conjunction "and" (one of the FANBOYS) links the two clauses correctly.

questions.q: What does the acronym FANBOYS refer to in the context of correcting run-ons?
o: A list of common sentence fragments students should avoid using
The seven coordinating conjunctions: for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so
A punctuation rule specifically for using semicolons correctly
The seven subordinating conjunctions taught in English grammar
questions.e: FANBOYS stands for the coordinating conjunctions for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so — used with a comma to correct a run-on.

questions.q: "The bus stopped suddenly; I found myself in an old man's lap." uses which correction method?
o: Period and a capital letter, with no conjunction at all
Subordinating conjunction, added right at the start
Semicolon, used all on its own
Comma and coordinating conjunction used together
questions.e: A semicolon is used to connect the two independent thoughts directly, without a conjunction.

questions.q: "When the bus stopped suddenly, I found myself in an old man's lap." uses which correction method?
o: A comma and a coordinating conjunction, used together
A semicolon, used entirely on its own
A period and a capital letter, with no conjunction
A subordinating conjunction, turning one clause into a dependent clause
questions.e: Adding the subordinating conjunction "when" turns the first clause into a dependent clause, joining the two thoughts into one complex sentence.

questions.q: Which of these is a correctly punctuated fix for "Akosua cleans her kitchen every week she shines every pot and pan." using a coordinating conjunction?
o: Akosua cleans her kitchen every week, and she shines every pot and pan.
Akosua cleans her kitchen every week and, she shines every pot and pan.
Akosua, cleans her kitchen every week and she shines every pot and pan.
Akosua cleans her kitchen every week; and she shines every pot and pan.
questions.e: The comma-and-coordinating-conjunction method places a comma directly before "and": "Akosua cleans her kitchen every week, and she shines every pot and pan."

questions.q: What does parallelism require of items arranged in a series?
o: That they be joined together only by semicolons
That they be the same grammatical category, form, and function
That they always be nouns, and only nouns
That there always be exactly two items in the series
questions.e: Parallelism means items in a series must share the same grammatical category (e.g. all verbs), the same grammatical form (e.g. all −ing), and perform the same grammatical function.

questions.q: Which sentence demonstrates correct parallelism?
o: Dance, singing and to write are my hobbies.
Dancing, sang and writing are my hobbies.
Dancing, singing and writing are my hobbies.
Dancing, to sing and writing are my hobbies.
questions.e: All three items — dancing, singing, writing — are −ing (gerund) forms, so they are parallel.

questions.q: Faulty parallelism arises when:
o: A sentence uses a semicolon in the wrong place entirely
A sentence lacks a subject entirely, with no noun present
A sentence has only one single item in its whole list
Items arranged in a series are of different grammatical forms or functions
questions.e: Faulty parallelism is the error of mixing different grammatical forms or functions among items that should match, in a series.

questions.q: "Of all the sports I've played, I prefer tennis, handball, and playing golf." is faulty because:
o: It mixes two nouns with a −ing phrase
It uses the wrong preposition throughout the sentence
It lacks a subject entirely, with no noun present
It has too many items listed in the series
questions.e: Tennis and handball are nouns, but "playing golf" is a gerund phrase — the series is not grammatically parallel.

questions.q: How could "Of all the sports I've played, I prefer tennis, handball, and playing golf." best be revised for parallelism?
o: I prefer tennis and handball, but I also am playing golf.
I prefer tennis, handball, and golf.
I prefer to play tennis, playing handball, and golf.
I prefer, tennis handball and playing golf.
questions.e: Making all three items nouns — tennis, handball, and golf — restores parallel structure.

questions.q: "He is a good choice for manager because he works hard, he keeps calm and well-liked." is an example of faulty parallelism because:
o: It repeats the word "he" far too many times
It is missing a subject entirely, with no noun present
It mixes two clauses with an adjective phrase
It has no verbs at all present in it
questions.e: Two full clauses are mixed with a bare adjective ("well-liked"), breaking the parallel structure of the series.

questions.q: Which is a correctly parallel revision of "He is a good choice for manager because he works hard, he keeps calm and well-liked."?
o: He is a good choice for manager because working hard, he keeps calm and well-liked.
He is a good choice for manager, he works hard he keeps calm and well-liked.
He is a good choice for manager because he works hard he keeps, calm and well-liked.
He is a good choice for manager because he works hard, keeps calm, and is well-liked.
questions.e: Making all three items verb phrases sharing the same subject "he" (works hard, keeps calm, is well-liked) restores parallelism.

questions.q: A shift construction is best described as:
o: An example of faulty parallelism — a sudden, unexpected change in point of view, tense, voice, or level of diction
A type of sentence fragment, lacking a subject or a main verb
A punctuation mark used to join two independent clauses together
A completely unrelated grammar error with no real connection to parallelism
questions.e: A shift construction is a form of faulty parallelism: an unexpected, inconsistent change in person, number, tense, voice, or mood that confuses the reader.

questions.q: In grammar, "person" refers to the distinction among:
o: Singular and plural forms only, nothing else at all
The person talking, the person spoken to, and the person/thing talked about
Active and passive voice used in the verb
Past, present and future tense used in the verb
questions.e: Person distinguishes first person (I, we), second person (you), and third person (he, she, they, one, a person, people).

questions.q: "If a person works hard, you can gain recognition." contains what kind of error?
o: A shift in tense
A shift in voice
A shift in person
A shift in mood
questions.e: The sentence mixes third person ("a person") with second person ("you") — a shift in person.

questions.q: Which revision of "If a person works hard, you can gain recognition." is considered the best, most natural fix?
o: If you work hard, a person can gain recognition.
If a person works hard, a person can gain recognition.
If a person works hard, you can gain recognition.
If people work hard, they can gain recognition.
questions.e: "If people work hard, they can gain recognition." uses consistent third person plural throughout, and reads more naturally than the singular "he or she" alternative.

questions.q: "People should not drive when they have been drinking." and "You should not drive when you have been drinking." share the same meaning but differ in:
o: Point of view, first vs second person
Voice, active vs passive
Mood, indicative vs imperative
Tense, past vs present
questions.e: Both sentences convey the same meaning, but from different points of view — one third person plural, the other second person — this is the person distinction.

questions.q: According to this topic, when is it acceptable to use "one," "you," or "people/they" to refer to people in general?
o: Never — only the single word "people" may ever be used in any context at all, without exception
Any of the three is acceptable on its own in an appropriate context, but mixing them within a sentence or passage is inconsistent
Only the word "you" is ever acceptable, in any register whatsoever, without exception
Only the word "one" is ever acceptable, and only in the most formal writing
questions.e: Any of the possibilities (third person generic, or second person) is acceptable individually in the right context; the error occurs only when they are mixed together.

questions.q: In grammar, "number" refers to the distinction between:
o: First and second person
Active and passive voice
Singular and plural
Fact and command
questions.e: Number is the distinction between singular (one) and plural (more than one).

questions.q: "If a student does not understand a lesson, they should consult the instructor." contains what kind of error?
o: A shift in voice, going from active to passive within the sentence
A shift in mood, going from indicative to imperative within the sentence
A run-on sentence, joined together without any punctuation at all
A shift in number, since the singular "a student" does not agree with the plural pronoun "they"
questions.e: "A student" is singular but "they" is plural — the pronoun does not agree in number with its antecedent.

questions.q: Which is a correctly revised version of "If a student does not understand a lesson, they should consult the instructor."?
o: If students do not understand a lesson, they should consult the instructor.
If a student does not understand a lesson, student should consult the instructor.
If the students does not understand a lesson, they should consult the instructor.
If a student does not understand a lesson, they should consult the instructor.
questions.e: Making the antecedent plural ("students") agrees with the plural pronoun "they," fixing the shift in number.

questions.q: "A student who does not understand a lesson should consult the instructor." fixes the number-shift problem by:
o: Adding a semicolon somewhere in the middle of the sentence
Rewriting the sentence to avoid the pronoun mismatch entirely, keeping everything singular
Changing the word "instructor" to the plural "instructors" instead
Changing the verb tense used throughout the whole sentence
questions.e: This revision avoids the plural pronoun altogether, keeping the subject singular throughout the sentence.

questions.q: Pronoun-antecedent number inconsistency, as seen in shift-in-number errors, occurs most often:
o: Between a subject and its complement
Between two independent clauses
Between a pronoun and its antecedent
Between a verb and its object
questions.e: Number inconsistency occurs most often between a pronoun (e.g. "they") and the antecedent it refers back to (e.g. "a student").

questions.q: What is the rule for verb tense across a sentence, paragraph, or essay?
o: Only present tense may ever be used, in any context
Only past tense is ever grammatically correct to use
Tense should change every single sentence for variety
Tense should be maintained consistently unless the meaning requires a change
questions.e: Consistency in verb tense should be maintained throughout a passage unless the meaning genuinely calls for a tense change.

questions.q: "The virus mutated so quickly that it develops a resistance to most vaccines." contains what kind of error?
o: A shift in tense
A shift in voice
A shift in person
A missing-subject fragment
questions.e: The verb shifts from past tense ("mutated") to present tense ("develops") without any change in meaning requiring it — a shift in tense.

questions.q: How is "The virus mutated so quickly that it develops a resistance to most vaccines." correctly revised?
o: The virus mutated so quickly, it is developing a resistance to most vaccines, and it developed one before.
The virus mutates so quickly that it develops a resistance to most vaccines.
The virus mutated so quickly that it developed a resistance to most vaccines, and it will develop more.
The virus will mutate so it developed resistance.
questions.e: Making both verbs present tense ("mutates" ... "develops") removes the inconsistent shift.

questions.q: "The city's crime rate continues to decrease, but experts disagreed on the reasons." contains what kind of error?
o: A shift in voice
A shift in mood
A shift in tense
A shift in number
questions.e: "Continues" is present tense while "disagreed" is past tense — an unnecessary shift in tense.

questions.q: What is the corrected version of "The city's crime rate continues to decrease, but experts disagreed on the reasons."?
o: The city's crime rate will continue to decrease, but experts disagreed on the reasons.
The city's crime rate continues to have decreased, but experts disagreed.
The city's crime rate continued to decrease, but experts disagree on the reasons.
The city's crime rate continues to decrease, but experts disagree on the reasons.
questions.e: Keeping both verbs in the present tense ("continues" ... "disagree") removes the inconsistency.

questions.q: In the active voice, the subject of the sentence:
o: Performs the action described by the verb
Must always be a pronoun of some kind
Is acted upon by the verb instead
Is always omitted from the sentence
questions.e: In the active voice, the subject performs the action of the verb (e.g. "The committee approved the plan.").

questions.q: In the passive voice, the subject of the sentence:
o: Performs the action of the verb itself
Is acted upon by the verb
Must always be plural in number
Is never stated anywhere in the sentence
questions.e: In the passive voice, the subject receives or is acted upon by the action (e.g. "The plan was approved by the committee.").

questions.q: "Internet newsgroups cover an enormous range of topics for discussion. Forums for meeting people with like interests are provided in these groups." contains what kind of error?
o: A comma splice
A shift in mood
A shift in voice
A shift in number
questions.e: "Cover" is active voice (newsgroups do the covering), but "are provided" is passive voice — an unnecessary shift in voice.

questions.q: How is the newsgroups example correctly revised to remove the shift in voice?
o: Forums for discussion topics are covered by Internet newsgroups and are provided for meeting people.
Internet newsgroups are covering topics and forums are provided.
Discussion topics are covered, and forums for meeting people are also being provided by newsgroups.
Internet newsgroups cover an enormous range of topics for discussion and provide forums for meeting people with like interests.
questions.e: Keeping both verbs active ("cover" ... "provide") with the same subject ("Internet newsgroups") removes the voice shift.

questions.q: "Drought and windstorms made farming impossible and many families were forced to leave Okom village due to starvation." contains what kind of error?
o: A shift in voice
A shift in tense
A shift in person
A dependent-word fragment
questions.e: "Made" is active voice, but "were forced" is passive voice — an inconsistent shift in voice within the same sentence.

questions.q: What does "mood" indicate about a sentence?
o: Whether it is long or short in its overall length
Whether the sentence states a fact/asks a question, gives a command, or expresses a condition/suggestion
The emotional tone of the writer expressing the idea
Whether the sentence uses active or passive voice throughout
questions.e: Mood shows whether the sentence is indicative (statement/question), imperative (command/direction), or subjunctive (condition/suggestion).

questions.q: Shifts in mood occur most frequently in which type of writing, according to this topic?
o: Question-and-answer dialogues, as found in a script
Poetry, especially free verse without a fixed rhyme
Directions, when the writer moves between the imperative and the indicative mood
Formal letters, especially business correspondence
questions.e: Shifts in mood most often occur in directions/instructions, where a writer inconsistently mixes imperative commands with indicative statements.

questions.q: "Cook the mixture slowly, and you should stir it until the sugar is dissolved." contains what kind of error?
o: A shift in tense
A shift in voice
A shift in number
A shift in mood
questions.e: "Cook" is an imperative command, but "you should stir" switches to the indicative mood — an inconsistent shift in mood.

questions.q: Which is the correctly revised, consistently imperative version of the cooking instruction?
o: Cook the mixture slowly and stir it until the sugar is dissolved.
You should cook the mixture slowly, and you should stir it until the sugar is dissolved.
The mixture should be cooked slowly and stirred until the sugar is dissolved.
Cooking the mixture slowly, stirring it until the sugar was dissolved.
questions.e: Dropping "you should" and using the base-form command "stir" keeps both verbs in the imperative mood, matching "cook."

questions.q: Which word class names a person, place, thing, or idea?
o: Noun
Verb
Adverb
Preposition
questions.e: Nouns are the word class used to name people, places, things, and abstract ideas.

questions.q: A word that describes or modifies a noun is called a(n):
o: Adjective
Adverb
Conjunction
Interjection
questions.e: Adjectives modify nouns by describing their qualities, such as size, color, or number.

questions.q: Which of the following is a coordinating conjunction?
o: But
Although
Because
Since
questions.e: "But" is one of the FANBOYS coordinating conjunctions (for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so).

questions.q: An auxiliary verb is used to:
o: Help form tense, mood, or voice with a main verb
Replace a noun entirely
Modify an adjective
Join two clauses
questions.e: Auxiliary (helping) verbs like "be", "have", and "do" combine with a main verb to build various tenses and structures.

questions.q: Which word class typically answers the question "how", "when", or "where"?
o: Adverb
Noun
Pronoun
Article
questions.e: Adverbs of manner, time, and place answer these questions about the action of a verb.

questions.q:
Read the passage, then answer: No one would believe that Emeka and Victor were twins; they were totally different from each other. Although Emeka was only ten minutes older than his twin brother, relatives seemed ridiculously obsessed with this sheer accident of their birth. Mother, father, aunties and uncles regularly drummed the point into Victor's head. They told him, in no uncertain terms, that, in the patrilineal set-up of their society, he had to succumb to the whims and caprices of Emeka, because the latter was the first-born son of the family. Everyone wondered how it was that Victor could be calmness personified, while his twin brother was as boisterous as he was aggressive. Their classmates concealed their regard for Victor in their unlikely taunt, "Young old man". When their mother was going away for a fortnight, she called all four of her children and told them that she had to leave everything in Emeka's hands. He let hell loose in the form of rowdy parties, eating sprees, video sessions… the complete works! When, by Saturday of the first week, the children found the food cupboard totally empty, because its contents had been gobbled down by Emeka's gang, Victor realized it was time for him to do something. Without making any fuss, he took his sisters to their aunt's house to eat once a day. The girls were never really full, but Victor convinced them that one always made sacrifices and bore discomfort bravely when one's mother was away. He could not bear was Victor's silent scorn and utter contempt for him. "Damn Victor," he swore vulgarly, and wished he could infect this paragon with his wild ways. As soon as their mother returned, the girls launched into an elaborate account of conditions under Emeka's "regime". Just as the girls finished complaining, Emeka sauntered into the house. Nobody said anything to him. In fact, you could hear a pin drop. The silence was far worse than a slap would have been.
Question: What does the extract "You could hear a pin drop" mean in context?
o: The house was very quiet.
They could literally hear a pin fall.
Everyone was listening carefully.
The house was empty.
